Subsets of Fₚ with two prescribed moments, Part II: every exponent — the classification, the Cauchy-Liouville-Mirimanoff polynomials that decide the column n=3, and where this moment subset sum stops being PORC

🏷️ Arithmetic geometry over finite fields · subsets with prescribed power sums

Carles Marín

At a glance

What the paper contributes

Ck(n,p) counts the n-subsets of 𝔽p with Σt = Σtk = 0. Part I settled k = 3; this note settles every k ≥ 3.

  • The singularity criterion (Proposition 2, Theorem 4): for a length-four stratum, singularity depends on k only through gcd(k−1, 6), by Mann's theorem, and the set of n with all length-four strata singular takes exactly three values.
  • …is the wrong criterion (Proposition 5): what kills weight one is a genus-zero normalisation; at k = 5, n = 6 a singular stratum has genus 5. With the corrected criterion, Ck(n,p) is Artin–Tate exactly for n ∈ {3,4,6} (k = 3), {3,4} (k = 5) and n = 3 otherwise (Theorem 8), and the surviving counts are written down (Theorem 9, Proposition 11).
  • The column n = 3 (Theorem 12, Propositions 15–16, Corollary 17): one term per root of Qk whose cubic Y³ + uY − u splits; elementary exactly for k ∈ {3, 4, 5, 7}, because deg Qk + 1 = dim M2k(SL2(ℤ)).
  • Not PORC (Proposition 13, Lemmas 14 and 21): some fibre has group S3 — unconditionally, with forty printed certificates for 6 ≤ k ≤ 46 — and a permutation-character identity shows it cannot cancel. Observation 20 separates the two failures of PORC by weight (Isham has the coexistence).
  • The polynomials Qk and the reduction to u are Helou's, Tzermias's and Nanninga's; the paper claims the arithmetic over 𝔽p.

🚀 Start here: Theorem 8: Cₖ(n,p) is Artin–Tate exactly for n ∈ 3,4,6 (k = 3), 3,4 (k = 5), 3 (every other k).

Main results:

  • Theorem 8: Cₖ(n,p) is Artin–Tate exactly for n ∈ 3,4,6 (k = 3), 3,4 (k = 5), 3 (every other k)
  • Theorem 12: the column n = 3 for every k, through Qₖ; elementary exactly for k ∈ 3, 4, 5, 7
  • Corollary 17: Cₖ(3,p) is elementary iff dim M₂ₖ(SL₂(Z)) = 1, i.e. at the weights 6, 8, 10, 14

📐 Setting (copied from the paper, abstract, §1–§6)

(Abstract) Fix \(k\ge 3\) and an odd prime \(p\), and let \(C_k(n,p)\) count the \(n\)-subsets \(T\subseteq {\mathbb {F}}_p\) with \(\sum _{t\in T}t=\sum _{t\in T}t^{k}=0\). (§1) The Li–Wan partition sieve attaches to each partition \(\lambda =(w_1,\dots ,w_l)\vdash n\) the variety

\[ V_\lambda \; =\; \Bigl\{ \, \textstyle \sum _i w_ix_i=0,\ \ \sum _i w_ix_i^{k}=0\, \Bigr\} \ \subset \ \mathbf P^{\, l-1}. \]

(§2) Throughout, write \(m=k-1\) and \(\mu _m\) for the \(m\)-th roots of unity. (§3) For \(\lambda =(w_1,\dots ,w_l)\vdash n\) put

\[ A_\lambda =\Bigl\{ x\in \mathbf A^{l}:\ \textstyle \sum _iw_ix_i=0,\ \sum _iw_ix_i^{k}=0\Bigr\} , \qquad z_\lambda =\prod _j j^{m_j}\, m_j!\, , \]

with \(m_j\) the number of parts of \(\lambda \) equal to \(j\), so that \(A_\lambda \) is the affine cone over \(V_\lambda \). (§5) Write \(\chi _p(a)=\bigl(\tfrac ap\bigr)\). (§6) Under \(e_1=0\) Newton’s recursion reads \(s_k=-e_2s_{k-2}+e_3s_{k-3}\) with \(s_1=0\), \(s_2=-2e_2\), \(s_3=3e_3\), so each \(s_k\) is a polynomial in \(e_2,e_3\). […] every factor of \(s_k\) other than \(e_2\) and \(e_3\) is a polynomial \(Q_k\) in \(u=e_2^{3}/e_3^{2}\).

\[ f_u(Y)\; =\; Y^{3}+uY-u, \qquad \text{so that}\qquad e_2=e_3=u,\quad \frac{e_2^{3}}{e_3^{2}}=u,\quad \operatorname {disc}f_u=-u^{2}(4u+27). \]
\[ \mathfrak D_k\; =\; \operatorname {lc}(Q_k)\cdot \operatorname {disc}(Q_k)\cdot \operatorname {Res}\bigl(Q_k,\; u(4u+27)\bigr)\ \in \ {\mathbb {Z}}\smallsetminus \{ 0\} . \]

Abstract.

Fix \(k\ge 3\) and an odd prime \(p\), and let \(C_k(n,p)\) count the \(n\)-subsets \(T\subseteq {\mathbb {F}}_p\) with \(\sum _{t\in T}t=\sum _{t\in T}t^{k}=0\). The companion note  [ 37 ] evaluates \(C_3(n,p)\) and shows it is elementary — a polynomial in \(p\) with coefficients in quadratic characters of fixed integers — exactly for \(n=3,4,6\). We settle every \(k\). Three things happen, and only the first is what \(k=3\) would lead one to expect. First, the criterion for the deciding stratum to be singular depends on \(k\) only through \(\gcd (k-1,6)\), by Mann’s theorem on relations between roots of unity, and takes exactly three values. Second, that criterion is not the right one: for plane cubics, singularity forces a genus-zero normalisation, which is why it controls the answer when \(k=3\), and the correct condition in general is that the normalisation have genus zero. Third, with the corrected criterion the classification collapses: \(C_k(n,p)\) is Artin–Tate precisely for \(n\in \{ 3,4,6\} \) when \(k=3\), for \(n\in \{ 3,4\} \) when \(k=5\), and for \(n=3\) alone in every other \(k\). We give the closed forms that survive, and we describe the column \(n=3\) completely: writing \(u=e_2^3/e_3^2\), the count is governed by the roots of an explicit polynomial \(Q_k(u)\) together with the cubic \(Y^3+uY-u\) attached to each root, and it is expressible in quadratic characters if and only if \(Q_k\) is constant, which happens exactly for \(k\in \{ 3,4,5,7\} \). That list is not accidental: \(\deg Q_k+1=\dim M_{2k}(\mathrm{SL}_2({\mathbb {Z}}))\), so the count is elementary exactly when that space of modular forms is one-dimensional, which happens at the weights \(6,8,10,14\); the exceptional return at weight \(14\) reflects the gap \(M_2=0\) after the first cusp form appears in weight \(12\). Where it is not elementary, some fibre of \(Q_k\) has Galois group \(S_3\), and a permutation-character identity shows the nonabelian part cannot cancel, so the count is not PORC. Finally we observe that the two ends of this classification fail to be polynomial on residue classes for different reasons: at \(n=3\), \(k=6\) the obstruction is a nonabelian Artin-type class function and the count takes two values, so it is polynomial on Frobenius sets; for \(n\ge 4\) the obstruction is a surviving weight-one Frobenius trace coming from a positive-genus curve, and there the count is not even POFS.

Keywords: moment subset sum; finite fields; prescribed moments; Li–Wan sieve; vanishing sums of roots of unity; Mann’s theorem; PORC; POFS; Artin–Tate counts; modular forms; elliptic curves; Mirimanoff’s conjecture; Cauchy–Liouville–Mirimanoff polynomials.

MSC 2020: 11T06, 11T24, 11G20, 14G15, 11R18.

1 What changes when the exponent changes

The counts \(C_J(n,p)\) for a general index set \(J\) were introduced in Part II of the separate \(S\)-matrix series  [ 38 ] , which proves the estimate \(C_J(n,p)=p^{-|J|}\binom pn+O_n(p^{n/2})\) and leaves the closed form open; the companion note  [ 37 ] closes the pair \(\{ 1,3\} \). Nothing in its mechanism used the number \(3\): the Li–Wan partition sieve  [ 21 ] attaches to each partition \(\lambda =(w_1,\dots ,w_l)\vdash n\) the variety

\begin{equation} \tag {1} V_\lambda \; =\; \Bigl\{ \, \textstyle \sum _i w_ix_i=0,\ \ \sum _i w_ix_i^{k}=0\, \Bigr\} \ \subset \ \mathbf P^{\, l-1}, \end{equation}
1

and a point of \(V_\lambda \) is singular exactly when its coordinates are \((k-1)\)-st roots of unity with \(\sum _iw_i\zeta _i=0\). For \(k=3\) those roots are signs, the condition reads “the weights split into two blocks of equal sum”, and that is a statement about partitions. For general \(k\) it is a statement about vanishing weighted sums of roots of unity, which is a different and much better-studied kind of object.

So the natural question is whether the answer for general \(k\) is the \(k=3\) answer with the signs replaced by roots of unity. It is not, and it fails twice — once in the arithmetic and once in the geometry. The arithmetic failure is mild and pleasant: the answer turns out to depend on \(k\) only through \(\gcd (k-1,6)\), so there are three cases and not infinitely many (Section 2). The whole answer is Figure 1, and the rest of this note is its proof. The geometric failure is the interesting one: the criterion “every length-four curve is singular”, which is what the \(k=3\) argument literally proves, is the wrong criterion, and it happens to be equivalent to the right one only when \(k=3\) (Section 3). Once corrected, the classification is short (Section 4) and the surviving counts can all be written down (Section 5).

🖼️ Figure 1

The result of this note. A cell is live when \(C_k(n,p)\) is Artin–Tate. The column \(n=3\) never dies, because a zero-dimensional variety always contributes an Artin character; but the class function is expressible in quadratic characters only for \(k\in \{ 3,4,5,7\} \) (Theorem 12), so “Artin–Tate” and “elementary” part company from \(k=6\) on. Among the nonabelian cells the two shades are not decoration: the darker ones, \(k=6\) and \(k=9\), are those where the group of the class function is exactly \(S_3\), and the paler ones those where it is larger: \(S_3\times C_2\) for \(k=8,10,11\), and not determined here for \(k=12\). Which cells are which, and why, is settled after Theorem 12; Proposition 13 gives one \(S_3\) fibre whenever \(\deg Q_k{\gt}0\), which is weaker than either and is all Lemma 14 needs. Everything else is dead, and the row \(k=3\) of the companion note is the only one with more than two live cells.

🖼️ Figure 2

Where this note sits, and what it owes. Four strands of work that do not otherwise meet: the Cauchy–Liouville–Mirimanoff family, the arithmetic of vanishing sums of roots of unity, the counting of subsets with prescribed power sums, and the question of when a counting function stops being polynomial — in the order drawn. The argument below needs a piece from each — Helou and Tzermias for the family our polynomials turn out to be, Mann for the criterion, Li–Wan for the sieve, and the PORC/POFS vocabulary to say what the failure is — and the box on the right marks the part we claim, which is the smallest of the four.

What is ours

Figure 2 is the map. The singular locus of a weighted hyperplane section of a diagonal form is classical; we claim no part of it, and Section 2 says whose it is. Mann’s theorem is Mann’s. The vanishing of \(H^1\) in dimension at least two is Ghorpade–Lachaud’s. The sieve is Li–Wan’s.

What the note establishes is Theorem 4, the corrected criterion of Proposition 5, the classification of Theorem 8 with the closed forms of Theorem 9 and Proposition 11 that it leaves standing, the arithmetic of the column \(n=3\) in Theorem 12 and its reading as a dimension of modular forms in Corollary 17, Proposition 13 with the certificates behind it and Lemma 14, which is what carries it to a failure of PORC, and Remark 3.

Some things in this note are not new and we say so where they appear. The coexistence of the two failure modes of Section 6 is in Isham  [ 17 ] , whose separation of a bounded zero-dimensional contribution from a surviving Frobenius trace is the same distinction and is load-bearing in her argument; we add only the identification of the bounded mode as POFS. And neither the polynomials \(Q_k\) nor the reduction that produces them is ours: both are in [ 16 , 41 , 33 ] , as Section 6 sets out where they first appear. What we claim there is the arithmetic consequence over \({\mathbb {F}}_p\), not the polynomials. Every theorem, proposition, corollary and observation below carries a card saying which of the two it is, except Proposition 2, a step towards Theorem 4; so do Lemmas 1 and 14 and Remarks 3 and 10. Figure 2 says the same thing in one picture.

2 The criterion, and why only \(\gcd (k-1,6)\) matters

Throughout, write \(m=k-1\) and \(\mu _m\) for the \(m\)-th roots of unity.

Lemma 1 the singular locus; the case \(k=3\) is Segre’s
#
📕 p. 4📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

Let \(\lambda =(w_1,\dots ,w_l)\) with \(w_i\) positive and \(\sum _iw_i=n\), and let \(V_\lambda \) be as in (1) over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(0\) or \(p{\gt}\max (n,k)\). A point \(z\in V_\lambda \) is singular if and only if, after scaling, \(z_i\in \mu _m\) for every \(i\) and \(\sum _iw_iz_i=0\). All such singularities are ordinary double points.

🆕 Classical and new: not ours, cited: for k = 3 Segre; Elsenhans–Jahnel [EJdisc, Fact 2.8]; for arbitrary degree Dimca–Sticlaru [DS, Thm. 2.4].

↳ Used in: Proposition 5, 6

Proof ▼

\(V_\lambda \) is cut by a hyperplane \(H\) and the hypersurface \(F=\sum _iw_ix_i^k\). A point is singular iff the two differentials are proportional, i.e. \(kw_iz_i^{k-1}=\mu w_i\) for all \(i\) and some \(\mu \); since \(w_i\ne 0\) this says \(z_i^{k-1}=\mu /k\) is the same for all \(i\), and rescaling makes it \(1\). The point must also lie on \(H\), which is \(\sum _iw_iz_i=0\).

For the second statement, restrict to \(H\) the bilinear form \(B(u,v)=\sum _i(w_i/z_i)u_iv_i\), which is the Hessian of \(F\) at \(z\) up to a nonzero scalar because \(z_i^{k-2}=z_i^{-1}\). It is nondegenerate on the ambient space, and \(B(z,u)=\sum _iw_iu_i\), so the \(B\)-orthogonal of \(H\) is \(\langle z\rangle \). Since \(\sum _iw_iz_i=0\) we have \(z\in H\), whence \(\operatorname {rad}(B|_H)=\langle z\rangle \); modulo the radial direction the Hessian is nondegenerate, which is an ordinary double point.

[enhanced,sharp corners=downhill,boxrule=0.4pt,left=5pt,right=5pt, top=3pt,bottom=3pt,colback=fajeno!4,colframe=fajeno!55, fontupper=,before skip=6pt,after skip=8pt] fajenoLemma 1fajenonot ours — cited
For \(k=3\) the base case is Segre (1887); the statement in the pentahedral coordinates used here is Elsenhans–Jahnel  [ 6 , Fact 2.8 ] , whose Examples 2.9 are three of our \(V_\lambda \) with their node counts printed; for arbitrary degree and coefficients it is Dimca–Sticlaru  [ 4 , Thm. 2.4 ] . The proof is reproduced because the note needs the ordinary-double-point half explicitly for every \(k\), not because anything is claimed.

The condition \(\sum _iw_i\zeta _i=0\) with \(\zeta _i\in \mu _m\) is a vanishing sum of roots of unity with positive rational weights. For a stratum of length four — the only length that will matter — there are four terms, and that is exactly the regime that Mann settled.

Proposition 2 the invariant is \(\gcd (m,6)\)
#
📕 p. 4📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

Let \(\lambda \) have length four. Whether \(V_\lambda \) is singular depends on \(m\) only through \(\gcd (m,6)\).

🆕 Classical and new: a step towards Theorem 4, resting on Mann’s theorem [Mann, Thm. 1].

↳ Used in: 3, Theorem 4

Proof ▼

Decompose a vanishing relation \(\sum _{i=1}^{4}w_i\zeta _i=0\) into minimal vanishing subsums, a decomposition that never splits an individual term. A singleton cannot vanish, because \(|w_i\zeta _i|=w_i{\gt}0\); and a block of three would leave a singleton. So the only possibilities are that the relation is itself minimal, or that it splits as \(2+2\).

If it is minimal then, by Mann  [ 24 ] , all ratios of participating roots have order dividing \(\prod _{q\le 4\ \text{prime}}q=6\); rotating one root to \(1\) puts the rest in \(\mu _m\cap \mu _6=\mu _{\gcd (m,6)}\), and whether such a relation exists is then a condition on \(\gcd (m,6)\) alone. If instead it splits as \(2+2\), each pair satisfies \(w_i\zeta _i=-w_j\zeta _j\), so taking absolute values gives \(w_i=w_j\) and then \(\zeta _i=-\zeta _j\); this requires \(-1\in \mu _m\), that is \(2\mid m\), which is again a condition on \(\gcd (m,6)\) alone.

🛡️ Evidence & scope

  • Program: the witness 1 + (−1) + ζ₇ + (−ζ₇) = 0 in μ₁₄; vanishing pairs for m ≤ 24, weights ≤ 5; ten length-four partitions depend only on gcd(m,6) for m ≤ 24. gates/P3d_mann_minimalidad.py

Remark 3 the minimality hypothesis is where the work is
#

Uses

  • Proposition 2
📕 p. 5📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

It is worth saying why the second case must be treated separately rather than absorbed into the first. Mann’s theorem bounds the ratios inside a minimal subsum, not between two of them, and four terms splitting as \(2+2\) can have ratios of arbitrarily large order:

\[ 1+(-1)+\zeta _7+(-\zeta _7)=0 \]

is a vanishing sum of four roots of unity with positive rational weights in which one ratio has order \(7\). A proof of Proposition 2 that decomposed into minimal subsums and then applied Mann to the whole relation would be answering a different question. For four terms Mann’s bound is already sharp — the relation \(2\cdot 1+(-1)+\omega +\omega ^{2}=0\) realises a ratio of order exactly \(6\) — and the sharper bound of Conway and Jones  [ 23 , Thm. 5 ] , which requires \(l\ge \sum _{q\mid r}(q-2)+2\), agrees with it here and only improves on it from five terms onwards.

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

Measured: The witness above verified exactly in \(\mu _{14}\), together with the assertion that its subsum \(\{ 1,-1\} \) vanishes so that it is not minimal; the claim that a vanishing pair forces \(w_i=w_j\) and \(\zeta _i=-\zeta _j\) checked exhaustively for \(m\le 24\) and weights up to \(5\); and the singularity pattern of ten length-four partitions verified to depend only on \(\gcd (m,6)\) for \(m\le 24\). See gates/P3d_mann_minimalidad.py.

[enhanced,sharp corners=downhill,boxrule=0.4pt,left=5pt,right=5pt, top=3pt,bottom=3pt,colback=fnuestro!4,colframe=fnuestro!55, fontupper=,before skip=6pt,after skip=8pt] fnuestroRemark 3fnuestroours — it isolates a hypothesis the proof needs
The witness \(1+(-1)+\zeta _7+(-\zeta _7)=0\) refutes a step that is natural to take and easy to take wrongly: decomposing into minimal subsums and then applying Mann to the whole relation. It leaves Proposition 2 standing — the \(2+2\) case costs two lines — but the hypothesis it isolates is the one the length-four argument rests on.

Theorem 4 the trichotomy
#

Uses

  • Proposition 2
  • Proposition 2
📕 p. 5📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

For \(m\ge 1\) let \(S_m\) be the set of \(n\ge 3\) such that every \(\lambda \vdash n\) of length four has \(V_\lambda \) singular. Then

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle S_m=\begin{cases} \{ 3\} & \text{if } m \text{ is odd},\\ \{ 3,4,6\} & \text{if } 2\mid m,\ 3\nmid m,\\ \{ 3,4,5,6\} & \text{if } 6\mid m. \end{cases}}} \]

🆕 Classical and new: ours — an elementary consequence of Mann [Mann] and the triangle inequality (the paper’s card).

↳ Used in: Theorem 8

Proof ▼

There are no partitions of \(3\) of length four, so \(3\in S_m\) always. The remaining content is which of \((2,1,1,1)\), \((3,1,1,1)\), \((2,2,1,1)\) and \((1,1,1,1)\) admit a relation.

For \((1,1,1,1)\) the relation \(1+1-1-1=0\) works as soon as \(-1\in \mu _m\), i.e. \(2\mid m\); and for \(m\) odd no relation exists, since by Proposition 2 we may take \(m\in \{ 1,3\} \), and four unit-weight terms in \(\mu _3\) sum to zero only if each cube root of unity occurs equally often, which four terms cannot do. This is the condition \(4\in S_m\). The partition \((2,2,1,1)\) has the same relation when \(2\mid m\), and also \(2+2\omega +\omega ^{2}+\omega ^{2}=0\) when \(3\mid m\); that changes nothing, because whether \(6\in S_m\) is decided by \((3,1,1,1)\) below, which needs \(2\mid m\).

For \((2,1,1,1)\) there can be no proper vanishing subsum, because the weight \(2\) has no equal-weight partner; so the whole relation is minimal and, by Proposition 2, lives in \(\mu _6\) after normalising \(\zeta _1=1\). Inspection gives \((\zeta _2,\zeta _3,\zeta _4)\) a permutation of \((-1,\omega ,\omega ^2)\) with \(\omega \) a primitive cube root, and indeed \(2-1+\omega +\omega ^{2}=2-1-1=0\). Equivalently, in the polynomial form of the criterion, \(\Phi _6\) divides the weight polynomial:

\[ 2+X^{2}+X^{3}+X^{4}=(X^{2}-X+1)(X^{2}+2X+2). \]

So \((2,1,1,1)\) is singular exactly when \(6\mid m\), and then carries exactly six geometric singular points. Since \((2,1,1,1)\) is the only length-four partition of \(5\), this is precisely the condition \(5\in S_m\).

For \((3,1,1,1)\), equality in \(|3\zeta _1|=|\zeta _2+\zeta _3+\zeta _4|\) forces \(\zeta _2=\zeta _3=\zeta _4=-\zeta _1\), which needs \(-1\in \mu _m\); so \((3,1,1,1)\) is singular exactly when \(2\mid m\), with exactly one singular point. Since \((2,2,1,1)\) is singular whenever \(2\mid m\), this gives \(6\in S_m\iff 2\mid m\).

Finally, for \(n\ge 7\) the partition \((n-3,1,1,1)\) has \(n-3{\gt}3\), so \(|(n-3)\zeta _1|{\gt}|\zeta _2+\zeta _3+\zeta _4|\) and no relation can exist for any \(m\); hence no \(n\ge 7\) lies in \(S_m\).

🛡️ Evidence & scope

  • Program: S_m from the definition by exhaustive enumeration over μ_m⁴, 1 ≤ m ≤ 18, 3 ≤ n ≤ 10; the factorisation by Φ₆ exactly. gates/P3d_tricotomia_Sm.py

For each \(m=k-1\le m_{\max }\), the set \(S_m\) of \(n\le n_{\max }\) whose length-four strata are all singular, by searching \(\mu _m^4\) for a point with \(\sum \lambda _i z_i=0\) (Lemma 1) for every partition \(\lambda \) of \(n\) into four parts; then each \(m\) is compared with the answer Theorem 4 gives from \(\gcd (m,6)\) alone.

Measured: \(S_m\) recomputed from the definition by exhaustive enumeration over \(\mu _m^4\) for \(1\le m\le 18\) and \(3\le n\le 10\), with no exception; the collapse to four \(\gcd \) classes, and the factorisation above, verified exactly. See gates/P3d_tricotomia_Sm.py.

Proposition 2 and Theorem 4 together. What the picture shows and the statement does not is that the collapse is not injective: four \(\gcd \) classes produce only three answers, because \(\gcd =1\) and \(\gcd =3\) agree. The circled \(m=15\) is the case that kills the natural guess — having several prime divisors is not what buys the even-\(m\) answer. The sets drawn here are the \(S_m\) of the trichotomy — which \(n\) have a singular length-four stratum — and not the live cells of Figure 1: the two coincide only at \(k=3\), and Section 3 is about why.

3 The criterion above is the wrong one

Theorem 4 is a complete answer to the question “for which \(n\) is every length-four stratum singular?”. That question is the right one for \(k=3\) and the wrong one in general, and it is worth being precise about why.

We first fix the notation the rest of this section uses. For \(\lambda =(w_1,\dots ,w_l)\vdash n\) put

\[ A_\lambda =\Bigl\{ x\in \mathbf A^{l}:\ \textstyle \sum _iw_ix_i=0,\ \sum _iw_ix_i^{k}=0\Bigr\} , \qquad z_\lambda =\prod _j j^{m_j}\, m_j!\, , \]

with \(m_j\) the number of parts of \(\lambda \) equal to \(j\), so that \(A_\lambda \) is the affine cone over \(V_\lambda \). The Li–Wan sieve  [ 21 ] is then the exact identity

\begin{equation} \tag {2} C_k(n,p)\; =\; \sum _{\lambda \vdash n}\frac{(-1)^{\, n-l(\lambda )}}{z_\lambda }\, \# A_\lambda ({\mathbb {F}}_p), \end{equation}
5

counting each unordered \(n\)-subset once by inclusion–exclusion over the coincidence patterns of its elements. What obstructs an elementary formula is weight one surviving in the corresponding motivic sum,

\[ \mathcal M_{n,k}=\sum _{\lambda \vdash n}\frac{(-1)^{\, n-l(\lambda )}}{z_\lambda }\, e_c(A_\lambda ), \]

whose Frobenius trace is the right-hand side of (2). For a length-four stratum, \(V_\lambda \) is a plane curve \(C\), and the cone over it satisfies \(e_c(A_C)=1+({\mathbb {L}}-1)e(C)\). Here \(C\) need not be irreducible — the witness of (6) is a union of three lines and a residual curve — so we keep track of its components. If \(C\) is reduced with \(r\) geometric components, then \(e(C)=1-[H^1(C)]+[\Pi _C]{\mathbb {L}}\), where \(\Pi _C\) is the permutation representation of \(G_{\mathbb {Q}}\) on those components, of dimension \(r\), and hence

\begin{equation} \tag {3} e_c(A_C)=[\Pi _C]\, {\mathbb {L}}^{2}+(1-[\Pi _C])\, {\mathbb {L}}+(1-{\mathbb {L}})\, [H^1(C)] . \end{equation}
6

The first two terms are Artin–Tate and carry only even weights, so they cannot contribute weight one; taking \(r=1\) recovers the familiar \({\mathbb {L}}^{2}+(1-{\mathbb {L}})[H^1(C)]\), and nothing below depends on which case we are in.

What does need care is \([H^1(C)]\) itself. For a nodal curve, reducible or not, \(H^1(C)\) may carry weight zero as well, coming from the dual graph \(\Gamma _C\): irreducibility does not prevent it, as a nodal plane cubic shows: its normalisation is \(\mathbf P^1\), yet the node closes a loop in \(\Gamma _C\), and

\[ \# C({\mathbb {F}}_p)=p+1-\operatorname {Tr}\bigl(\operatorname {Frob}_p\mid H^1(\Gamma _C)\bigr), \]

which is \(p\) for a split node and \(p+2\) for a non-split one — in either case not \(p+1\). The two graded pieces are

\[ \operatorname {gr}^W_0H^1(C)\simeq H^1(\Gamma _C), \qquad \operatorname {gr}^W_1H^1(C)\simeq H^1(\widetilde C), \]

so “the weight-one part is \([H^1(C)]\)” would not be literally true; the statement that holds in both cases is

\[ \operatorname {gr}^W_1H^1(C)=H^1(\widetilde C), \]

\(\widetilde C\) the normalisation: the difference between \(e(C)\) and \(e(\widetilde C)\) is supported on the finite sets of nodes and branches, hence Artin of weight zero. Therefore

\begin{equation} \tag {4} { \boxed {\displaystyle \operatorname {gr}^W_1 e_c(A_C)=[H^1(\widetilde C)]}} \end{equation}
7

and singularity is not what kills weight one — rationality of the normalisation is.

For \(k=3\) the two coincide, because every geometric component of the normalisation of a reduced singular plane cubic has genus zero — the irreducible case is the usual rational parametrisation, and a reducible one splits into lines and conics. For \(k\ge 4\) they do not, and the smallest discrepancy is small enough to write out.

Proposition 5 the converse fails at \(k=5\), \(n=6\)
#

Uses

  • Lemma 1
  • Lemma 1
📕 p. 8📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

Let \(k=5\), so \(m=4\), and \(\lambda =(3,1,1,1)\). Then \(V_\lambda \) is a geometrically irreducible plane quintic with exactly one node, its normalisation has genus \(5\), and consequently \(C_5(6,p)\) is not elementary — although \(\lambda =(3,1,1,1)\) and the other length-four partition \((2,2,1,1)\) of \(6\) are both singular, so that \(6\in S_4\).

🆕 Classical and new: ours, and load-bearing (the paper’s card); it does not affect Part I, which is the case k = 3.

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

Proof ▼

The singular-point equation is \(3z_1+z_2+z_3+z_4=0\) with \(z_i\in \mu _4\); equality in the triangle inequality forces \([z_1:z_2:z_3:z_4]=[1:-1:-1:-1]\), so there is exactly one singular point, a node by Lemma 1. The quintic is geometrically irreducible: two groups of components of degrees \(a\) and \(5-a\) would meet in \(a(5-a)\ge 4\) points counted with multiplicity, and with all singularities ordinary nodes those intersections cannot be concentrated in the single available node. Hence \(g(\widetilde V_\lambda )=\tfrac {(5-1)(5-2)}2-1=5\), and \([H^1]\) has dimension \(10\). Since \(z_{(3,1,1,1)}=3\cdot 3!=18\), the summand \(\tfrac 1{18}[H^1(\widetilde V_\lambda )]\) appears in (4) with the sign common to the whole length-four stratum, so it cannot cancel; and an expression polynomial in \(p\) with fixed-character coefficients is Artin–Tate and has only even weights.

[enhanced,sharp corners=downhill,boxrule=0.4pt,left=5pt,right=5pt, top=3pt,bottom=3pt,colback=fnuestro!4,colframe=fnuestro!55, fontupper=,before skip=6pt,after skip=8pt] fnuestroProposition 5fnuestroours — and it is load-bearing
This is why “every four-part curve is singular” must be replaced by “every four-part curve has genus-zero normalisation”. For plane cubics, singularity forces a genus-zero normalisation; in higher degree singularity alone no longer does, which is the whole content of the correction — not that a node can never destroy weight one there, since a three-nodal plane quartic has geometric genus zero too, but that one has to count the singularities to know. It does not affect  [ 37 ] , which is the case \(k=3\); it does mean that the trichotomy of Theorem 4, taken alone, would predict \(6\in S_4\) and hence a closed form for \(C_5(6,p)\) that does not exist.

Two remarks are worth recording, because both bound what the method can claim.

Remark 6 the higher strata still contribute nothing of weight one, and why
#

Uses

  • Lemma 1
📕 p. 9📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

For \(l\ge 5\) the variety \(V_\lambda \) has dimension \(d=l-3\ge 2\) and is cut in \(\mathbf P^{l-1}\) by \(r=2\) forms, so Ghorpade–Lachaud  [ 7 , Prop. 3.2 ] gives \(H^i(\mathbf P^{l-1})\to H^i(V_\lambda )\) an isomorphism for \(i\le l-1-2-1=l-4\); taking \(i=1\) needs exactly \(l\ge 5\), and yields \(H^1(V_\lambda )=0\). Blowing up the nodes, the exceptional fibres are smooth quadrics of dimension \(d-1\ge 1\), connected and with vanishing \(H^1\), so proper base change gives \(H^1(Y_\lambda )=0\) on the resolution as well; the quadrics contribute only even weights. What must be stressed is that this uses that the singularities are nodes, supplied by Lemma 1; it is not an assertion about singular hypersurfaces in general.

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

Remark 7 “no weight one” does not mean “Artin–Tate”
#
📕 p. 9📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

At the same parameters \(k=5\), \(n=6\), take \(\lambda =(2,1,1,1,1)\). Then \(V_\lambda \) is a nodal quintic surface in \(\mathbf P^3\); its dualising sheaf is \(\mathcal O(1)\) and resolving ordinary double points preserves the geometric genus, so the resolution has \(h^{2,0}=4\). Its \(H^2\) is genuinely not Artin–Tate, even though \(H^1\) vanishes. The weight-one argument is therefore an obstruction and not a converse theorem: it can prove that a count fails to be elementary, never that it succeeds. Every positive statement below is proved by exhibiting the formula.

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

4 The classification

Theorem 8 all \(k\), all \(n\)
#

Uses

  • Proposition 11
  • Theorem 9
  • Theorem 4
  • Proposition 11
  • Theorem 9
  • Theorem 4
📕 p. 9📍 map❝ cite⚠ report
⚠ Erratum (2026-11-10): Editorial: in the bibliography, the first author of [GMPP] (Smooth symmetric systems over a finite field and applications) is N. Giménez, not «J. Giménez». No statement is affected.
⚠ Erratum (2026-11-10): Editorial: the legend drawn inside Figure 1 calls the paler nonabelian cells «nonabelian too, but the group is larger and not determined here»; the caption and the text determine the group, S₃ × C₂, for k = 8, 10, 11, and only k = 12 is left undetermined. No statement is affected.

Say \(C_k(n,p)\) is Artin–Tate if there are a number field \(L/{\mathbb {Q}}\) finite Galois with group \(\Gamma \), a number field \(E\) splitting \(\Gamma \), and class functions \(\alpha _0,\dots ,\alpha _d\) on \(\Gamma \) with values in \(E\) — equivalently, \(E\)-linear combinations of Artin characters — such that

\begin{equation} C_k(n,p)\; =\; \sum _{j=0}^{d}p^{\, j}\, \alpha _j(\operatorname {Frob}_p) \end{equation}
8

for all but finitely many \(p\). Then

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle \{ \, n\ge 3:\ C_k(n,p)\ \text{is Artin--Tate}\, \} = \begin{cases} \{ 3,4,6\} , & k=3,\\ \{ 3,4\} , & k=5,\\ \{ 3\} , & k\ne 3,5. \end{cases}}} \]

🆕 Classical and new: ours — proved, not extrapolated (the paper’s card); the case k = 3 is Part I [P3c, Thm. 6 and Remark 7].

↳ Used in: 20

Proof ▼

The case \(k=3\) is  [ 37 , Thm. 6 and Remark 7 ] : Theorem 6 there excludes elementary expressions for \(n\notin \{ 3,4,6\} \), and Remark 7 notes that the same weight-one argument excludes coefficients given by arbitrary Artin-type class functions of finite image, which is the class (5); for \(n=3,4,6\) the closed forms there are elementary, hence Artin–Tate. For \(n=3\) there are no length-four strata and every \(V_\lambda \) with \(\lambda \vdash 3\) is zero-dimensional, so the cones over them contribute only Artin–Tate classes and the count is an Artin-type class function in the sense of (5). It need not be a character: Proposition 11 produces the indicator of a conjugacy class, which is why (5) was stated for combinations rather than for traces. This is the column \(n=3\) of Figure 1, and Section 6 shows the class function need not be abelian. It remains to kill every \(n\ge 4\) when \(k\ne 3\), and every \(n\ge 5\) when \(k=5\).

Two uniform witnesses do it, and Figure 4 is the bookkeeping.

The witness at \(n=4\). Here \(\lambda =(1,1,1,1)\) and, eliminating \(x_4\), the curve is \(F_k(x,y,z)=x^k+y^k+z^k-(x+y+z)^k\). If \(k\) is even then \(m\) is odd, the curve is smooth by Theorem 4, and its genus is \(\binom {k-1}2\ge 3\). If \(k\) is odd then, up to a nonzero scalar,

\begin{equation} F_k=(x+y)(x+z)(y+z)\, R_{k-3}, \end{equation}
12

with \(R_{k-3}\) of degree \(k-3\). Every singular point of \(F_k\) corresponds to four unit roots summing to zero, hence lies on one of the three pairing lines; since all singularities are nodes, \(R_{k-3}\) can have no singularity — off the lines it would give an unaccounted singular point of \(F_k\), on a line it would give multiplicity at least three — and it cannot be reducible, by Bézout. So \(R_{k-3}\) is smooth of genus \(\binom {k-4}2\). This is positive for odd \(k\ge 7\) and zero exactly for \(k=3\) (no residual curve at all) and \(k=5\) (a conic). Hence \(n=4\) dies for every \(k\ne 3,5\), and survives for \(k=3,5\).

The witness at \(n\ge 5\). For \(n\ge 7\) take \(\lambda =(n-3,1,1,1)\), smooth for every \(m\) by the last paragraph of Theorem 4, of genus \(\binom {k-1}2{\gt}0\) for \(k\ge 4\). For \(n=6\) take \(\lambda =(3,1,1,1)\): smooth when \(k\) is even and carrying exactly one node when \(k\) is odd, so its normalisation has genus \(\binom {k-1}2\) or \(\binom {k-1}2-1\), positive for every \(k\ge 4\). For \(n=5\) take \(\lambda =(2,1,1,1)\): smooth unless \(6\mid m\), and when \(6\mid m\) it carries exactly six nodes, so with \(r\) geometric components \(\sum _jg(\widetilde C_j)=\binom {k-1}2-6+r-1\ge 9\) because \(6\mid m\) forces \(k\ge 7\).

In each case a length-four stratum has normalisation of positive genus, so by (4) the class \(\operatorname {gr}^W_1\mathcal M_{n,k}\) is a sum of effective classes with one common sign and is nonzero.

To conclude, fix an embedding \(\iota \colon E\hookrightarrow \overline{\mathbb {Q}}_\ell \). Read through \(\iota \), the right-hand side of (5) is not the trace of a representation — its coefficients are fractional, as \(\mathbf1_{\{ 1\} }=\tfrac 16\chi _{\mathrm{reg}}\) above already shows — but it is the trace of a well-defined virtual one, an element of the Grothendieck group

\[ K_0^{\mathrm{ss}}\bigl(G_{\mathbb {Q}},\overline{\mathbb {Q}}_\ell \bigr)\otimes _{{\mathbb {Z}}}E \]

of semisimple \(\overline{\mathbb {Q}}_\ell \)-representations with coefficients extended to \(E\). In that group the trace still determines the class, irreducible characters being \(E\)-linearly independent. Chebotarev gives agreement of traces at a set of primes of density one, so Brauer–Nesbitt forces agreement of the two classes there; and every weight occurring on the Artin–Tate side is even, while \(\operatorname {gr}^W_1\mathcal M_{n,k}\ne 0\). The comparison is thus between virtual representations throughout, which is all the weight argument needs. The positive direction for \(k=5\), \(n\in \{ 3,4\} \) is Section 5.

🧪 Lab: Figure 1 for your own range, and the counts of one cell

The grid of Theorem 8 for \(3\le k\le k_{\max }\), \(3\le n\le n_{\max }\) (the column \(n=3\) is split by \(\deg Q_k\), computed), and, for the cell \((k,n)\) you choose, \(C_k(n,p)\) counted over every \(n\)-subset of \(\mathbf F_p\). The counts are data; the verdict on the cell is the theorem.

🧪 Lab: Figure 4: the two witnesses, genus and singular points

The genera of the two witnesses of the proof of Theorem 8, \(\lambda =(1,1,1,1)\) for \(n=4\) and \(\lambda =(3,1,1,1)\) for \(n=6\), with what can be counted: the arithmetic genus of a plane curve of degree \(k\) and its singular points in \(\mu _{k-1}^4\) (Lemma 1). Where the two disagree, the curve is reducible.

Two features of this definition are chosen rather than inherited: the theorem needs the first; the second is what lets Observation 20 use it.

First, the \(\alpha _j\) are combinations of Artin characters and not traces of a single representation. Proposition 11 gives \(C_6(3,p)=(p-1)\mathbf1\{ \operatorname {Frob}_p=1\} \) with \(\Gamma =S_3\), and the indicator of the identity class is not the character of any representation: it is

\[ \mathbf1_{\{ 1\} }=\tfrac 16\chi _{\mathrm{reg}} =\tfrac 16\chi _{\mathrm{triv}}+\tfrac 16\chi _{\mathrm{sgn}}+\tfrac 13\chi _{\mathrm{std}}, \]

with fractional coefficients.

Second, the coefficient field must split \(\Gamma \), and \({\mathbb {Q}}\) will not do in general. The smallest witness is \(\Gamma =C_3=\langle g\rangle \), where \(\{ g\} \) is a conjugacy class on its own because the group is abelian, and

\[ \mathbf1_{\{ g\} }=\tfrac 13\bigl(1+\zeta _3^{-1}\chi +\zeta _3^{-2}\chi ^{2}\bigr), \qquad \chi (g)=\zeta _3 , \]

whose coefficients are not rational — and no other \({\mathbb {Q}}\)-combination of \(1,\chi ,\chi ^{2}\) equals it. Over a splitting field \(E\) the \(E\)-valued class functions are exactly the \(E\)-combinations of irreducible characters, so (5) then contains every indicator of a union of conjugacy classes. The class of Artin–Tate functions is a ring containing all of them, hence contains every function polynomial on Frobenius sets — POFS in the sense of  [ 47 , § 1.5.2 ] — and a fortiori every PORC function. The weight argument does not notice the change: fix an embedding \(E\hookrightarrow \overline{\mathbb {Q}}_\ell \) and read (5) there.

That is what makes the theorem worth stating in this form: a single weight-one obstruction rules out all three classes at once, and Observation 20 does not need a separate argument for POFS. [enhanced,sharp corners=downhill,boxrule=0.4pt,left=5pt,right=5pt, top=3pt,bottom=3pt,colback=fnuestro!4,colframe=fnuestro!55, fontupper=,before skip=6pt,after skip=8pt] fnuestroTheorem 8fnuestroours — proved, not extrapolated
The witnesses are uniform in \(n\) and \(k\), so no computation is being extended past its range. What it rests on — the trichotomy, the weight-one reduction (4), the factorisation (6), the node counts of \((3,1,1,1)\) and \((2,1,1,1)\) and the smoothness of \((n-3,1,1,1)\) — is proved above; the trichotomy is also verified by exhaustive enumeration in the range stated with it. For the higher strata the cohomological input is Ghorpade–Lachaud  [ 7 , Prop. 3.2 ] , through Remark 6; the comparison of classes uses Chebotarev and Brauer–Nesbitt.

5 The counts that survive

Theorem 8 asserts three closed forms beyond those of  [ 37 ] . Here they are; Table 2 collects them together with those of the companion note and records, for each, the reason the length-four obstruction failed to appear. Write \(\chi _p(a)=\bigl(\tfrac ap\bigr)\).

Theorem 9
#
📕 p. 11📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

For \(p{\gt}3\),

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle C_4(3,p)=\frac{(p-1)\bigl(1+\chi _p(-3)\bigr)}{6}}},\qquad { \boxed {\displaystyle C_5(3,p)=\frac{(p-1)\bigl(4+\chi _p(-3)\bigr)}{6}}}, \]

and

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle C_5(4,p)=\frac{p-1}{24}\Bigl(4p-17-6\chi _p(-2)-3\chi _p(-1)\Bigr)}} . \]

At \(p=3\) the three counts are \(0\), \(1\) and \(0\); the two formulas for \(k=5\) also hold at \(p=5\), where they give \(2\) and \(1\).

🆕 Classical and new: ours — identities, not fits; the first recovers the size-three super-Vandermonde sets of Sziklai and Takáts [ST, Thm. 1.12].

↳ Used in: Theorem 8

Proof ▼

Write \(e_j\) for the elementary symmetric functions of the elements of \(T\) and \(s_j\) for the power sums. Under \(e_1=0\), Newton’s identities give \(s_4=2e_2^2\) and \(s_5=-5e_2e_3\).

For three elements and \(s_4=0\) one gets \(e_2=0\), and the distinct triples with \(e_1=e_2=0\) are exactly the sets \(a\{ 1,\omega ,\omega ^2\} \) with \(\omega \) a primitive cube root, which exist iff \(\chi _p(-3)=1\); there are \((p-1)/3\) of them in that case and \(0\) otherwise, which is the first formula.

For three elements and \(s_5=0\), away from characteristic \(5\), either \(e_2=0\) or \(e_3=0\). The triples with \(e_3=0\) and \(e_1=0\) are \(\{ 0,a,-a\} \), of which there are \((p-1)/2\); the two families are disjoint, giving the second formula.

For four elements with \(e_1=0\) the identity \(s_5=-5e_2e_3\) still holds. Let \(A\) be the family with \(e_2=0\) and \(B\) the family with \(e_3=0\). Vanishing of \(e_3\) together with \(e_1=0\) makes the root polynomial even, so \(B=\{ \{ \pm a,\pm b\} : a,b\ne 0,\ b\ne \pm a\} \) and \(|B|=(p-1)(p-3)/8\). The condition \(e_2=0\) is the quadratic moment condition \(s_2=0\), whose distinct-coordinate sieve gives \(|A|=(p-1)\bigl(p-5-6\chi _p(-2)\bigr)/24\). The intersection consists of the sets \(\{ a,-a,ia,-ia\} \) with \(i^2=-1\), so \(|A\cap B|=(p-1)\bigl(1+\chi _p(-1)\bigr)/8\). Inclusion and exclusion give the third formula.

At \(p=5\) the argument for the two counts with \(k=5\) does not apply, since \(s_5=-5e_2e_3\) vanishes identically; but \(x^5=x\) on \({\mathbb {F}}_5\), so \(s_5=s_1\) and the only condition is \(s_1=0\). Translation by \(t\) shifts the sum of an \(n\)-subset by \(nt\), and \(n=3,4\) are invertible mod \(5\), so the \(\binom 5n\) subsets are spread evenly over the five sums: \(2\) for \(n=3\) and \(1\) for \(n=4\), which are the values of the two formulas.

Remark 10 the case \(k=4\) has a name, and is classified
#
📕 p. 12📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

For \(n=3\) and \(k=4\), Newton under \(e_1=0\) gives \(s_4=2e_2^2\), so the condition \(s_1=s_4=0\) is \(s_1=s_2=0\); a triple of distinct elements with \(s_1=s_2=0\) and \(s_3\ne 0\) is precisely a super-Vandermonde set of size three in the sense of Sziklai–Takáts  [ 45 ] , whose Theorem 1.12 shows that such a set of size \(t{\lt}p\) is a coset of a multiplicative subgroup — for \(t=3\), exactly the sets \(a\{ 1,\omega ,\omega ^2\} \) that the proof above produces. Our first formula therefore recovers a classification that has been available since 2008, by a different route; we claim nothing for it, and Blokhuis et al.  [ 22 ] is the current state of that line. What is not in that literature is our actual object: the invariant \(w_T\) there is by construction the first non-vanishing moment, so the prescribed condition is always an initial segment \(s_1=\dots =s_{t-1}=0\), whereas we prescribe \(s_1=s_k=0\) and leave everything between them free. Already at \(p=19\) and \(k=6\), all eighteen triples with \(s_1=s_6=0\) have \(s_2\ne 0\) and are therefore not Vandermonde sets of any kind.

The structure of the \(k=4\) triples is their Theorem 1.12, and the count \((p-1)/3\) is a one-line consequence of it. Our first closed form recovers both by a different route, and we say so where the formula appears rather than in a footnote. The remark earns its place for the second half: it identifies, in their own terms, why our object is not in their literature.

6 Two different failures, and only one of them is a trace

The column \(n=3\) of Figure 1 survives for every \(k\), because a zero-dimensional variety contributes an Artin character — a genuine one, \(H^0\) of a finite scheme being a permutation representation. That is a weaker statement than it looks, because the count is a combination of such characters and combinations need not be characters; the first place it bites is \(k=6\).

Proposition 11
#
📕 p. 13📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

For \(p\nmid 66\),

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle C_6(3,p)=(p-1)\cdot \mathbf1\bigl\{ \, 2Y^{3}+3Y-3\ \text{splits completely over } {\mathbb {F}}_p\, \bigr\} }} . \]

The cubic \(2Y^3+3Y-3\) is irreducible over \({\mathbb {Q}}\) with discriminant \(-1188=-36\cdot 33\), so its Galois group is \(S_3\) and complete splitting is not determined by any congruence on \(p\).

🆕 Classical and new: ours (the paper’s card).

↳ Used in: Theorem 8

Proof ▼

Newton with \(e_1=0\) gives \(s_6=-2e_2^3+3e_3^2\), and a solution with distinct entries has \(e_2e_3\ne 0\). So \(s_6=0\) says exactly

\[ \frac{e_2^{3}}{e_3^{2}}\; =\; \frac32 , \]

a condition on the scaling invariant alone. Scaling the three roots by \(t\) sends \(e_j\mapsto t^{\, j}e_j\), so \(t=e_2/e_3\) makes \(e_2\) and \(e_3\) equal, and their common value is \(e_2^{3}/e_3^{2}=\tfrac 32\): the normalised polynomial is \(Y^3+\tfrac 32Y-\tfrac 32\), one half of \(2Y^3+3Y-3\). When that splits, its nonzero scalings give exactly \(p-1\) distinct subsets. The discriminant is computed directly; it is not a square, so the Galois group is \(S_3\) and not \(C_3\), and Chebotarev distinguishes the identity class from a \(3\)-cycle inside any fixed cyclotomic congruence condition.

🛡️ Evidence & scope

  • Program: against exhaustive enumeration in the 17 primes 5 ≤ p ≤ 71 with p ∤ 66; density of split primes 0.160 below 400. gates/P3d_tricotomia_Sm.py

[enhanced,sharp corners=downhill,boxrule=0.4pt,left=5pt,right=5pt, top=3pt,bottom=3pt,colback=fnuestro!4,colframe=fnuestro!55, fontupper=,before skip=6pt,after skip=8pt] fnuestroProposition 11fnuestroours
The case \(k=6\) of Theorem 12, written out separately because it is the first \(k\) where the class function stops being abelian and because that fact is easy to miss. The discriminant \(-1188\) and the Galois group are a direct computation.

Proposition 11 is not an isolated accident, and the whole column can be described. Under \(e_1=0\) Newton’s recursion reads \(s_k=-e_2s_{k-2}+e_3s_{k-3}\) with \(s_1=0\), \(s_2=-2e_2\), \(s_3=3e_3\), so each \(s_k\) is a polynomial in \(e_2,e_3\). Since \(e_2\) has weight \(2\) and \(e_3\) weight \(3\), the scaling \(T\mapsto tT\) acts with \(e_2^3/e_3^2\) invariant, and every factor of \(s_k\) other than \(e_2\) and \(e_3\) is a polynomial \(Q_k\) in

\[ u\; =\; e_2^{3}/e_3^{2}. \]

Neither the polynomials nor this reduction are new, and it is worth saying exactly whose they are before using them. Parametrising an ordered projective triple as \([X:1:-X-1]\) turns the moment condition into \((X+1)^k-X^k-1=0\) for odd \(k\), whose non-cyclotomic factor is the Cauchy–Liouville–Mirimanoff polynomial \(E_k\), studied since  [ 13 ] and [ 32 ] . Helou  [ 16 , pp. 52–53 ] observed that its roots fall into orbits of six under an \(S_3\)-action, introduced the invariant \(J(X)=(X^2+X+1)^3/X^2(X+1)^2\) — which is our \(-u\), and is \(j/256\) in the coordinate \(\lambda =-X\) — and defined the quotient polynomial \(T_k\) with \(E_k=(-1)^{r_k}kX^{2r_k}(X+1)^{2r_k}T_k(6-J)\). Tzermias  [ 41 , (2.1)–(2.2) ] restates this as \(E_k=k(X^2+X)^{2r_k}T_k(J)\) with \(r_k=(k-3-2b)/6\), where \(b\) is the exponent of \(X^2+X+1\) in \((X+1)^k-X^k-1\), that is \(b=0,1,2\) for \(k\equiv 3,5,1\pmod6\); Nanninga  [ 33 , 34 ] develops the family, including the even-index analogue and a closed coefficient formula. The expansion of \(x^k+y^k+z^k\) for \(x+y+z=0\) that underlies all of this is older than the family itself: it is Todhunter’s  [ 43 ] , and Muir’s title  [ 44 ] names our object outright; further proofs are due to Carlitz–Hunter and to Wituła–Słota, it is carried with its proof in  [ 25 , pp. 227–229 ] , and Tzermias  [ 42 , Thm. 2.4 ] gives a modern one. For odd \(k\), our \(Q_k\) is \(T_k\) in primitive integral form, in the coordinate \(J=-u\): for \(k=9,15,21\) the coefficients agree with Tzermias’s table term by term, and the identification is verified coefficient by coefficient for every odd \(7\le k\le 45\). What follows is therefore not a statement about these polynomials but about what they count over \({\mathbb {F}}_p\).

Each value of the invariant \(u\) is realised by a canonical cubic, and fixing it once removes the only vagueness in the statement below. Write

\begin{equation} \tag {7} f_u(Y)\; =\; Y^{3}+uY-u, \qquad \text{so that}\qquad e_2=e_3=u,\quad \frac{e_2^{3}}{e_3^{2}}=u,\quad \operatorname {disc}f_u=-u^{2}(4u+27). \end{equation}
13

Any \(Y^3+aY-b\) with \(a^3/b^2=u\) is a scaling of \(f_u\), so which one is chosen does not affect whether it splits; \(f_u\) is the choice that makes the bad primes computable. The cubic that appeared in Proposition 11 is this one at \(u=\tfrac 32\): there the condition \(s_6=0\) pinned the invariant, and \(2f_{3/2}=2Y^3+3Y-3\). Put

\begin{equation} \tag {8} \mathfrak D_k\; =\; \operatorname {lc}(Q_k)\cdot \operatorname {disc}(Q_k)\cdot \operatorname {Res}\bigl(Q_k,\; u(4u+27)\bigr)\ \in \ {\mathbb {Z}}\smallsetminus \{ 0\} , \end{equation}
14

a nonzero integer whenever \(\deg Q_k{\gt}0\). That it is nonzero is proved in Appendix A, step one, which shows that the roots of \(Q_k\) are real, positive and simple: so no two coincide, and none is \(0\) or \(-27/4\). Its three factors exclude, in order, a root escaping to infinity mod \(p\), two roots colliding, and a root landing where \(f_u\) degenerates. For \(\deg Q_k=0\) set \(\mathfrak D_k=1\).

Theorem 12 the column \(n=3\)
#

Uses

  • Lemma 14
  • Proposition 15
  • Proposition 13
  • Lemma 14
  • Proposition 15
  • Proposition 13
📕 p. 14📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

For every prime \(p\nmid 6k\mathfrak D_k\),

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle \begin{aligned} \frac{6\, C_k(3,p)}{p-1} & =\bigl[e_2\mid s_k\bigr]\bigl(1+\chi _p(-3)\bigr)+3\bigl[e_3\mid s_k\bigr]\\[2pt]& \qquad +6\, \# \bigl\{ u_0\in {\mathbb {F}}_p:\ Q_k(u_0)=0,\ f_{u_0}\ \text{splits completely}\bigr\} \end{aligned}}} \]

with \(f_u\) as in (7). Consequently \(C_k(3,p)\) is elementary — expressible in quadratic characters of fixed integers — if and only if \(Q_k\) is constant, that is, if and only if \(s_k\) is a monomial in \(e_2\) and \(e_3\). That happens exactly for

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle k\in \{ 3,4,5,7\} }} . \]

🆕 Classical and new: ours — the count, not the polynomials: Q_k and the reduction to u are in Helou, Tzermias and Nanninga [Helou; Tzermias; NanA].

↳ Used in: Corollary 17

Proof ▼

The factor \(e_2\) contributes the triples with \(e_1=e_2=0\), which are the sets \(a\{ 1,\omega ,\omega ^2\} \) and number \((p-1)(1+\chi _p(-3))/6\); the factor \(e_3\) contributes \(\{ 0,a,-a\} \), of which there are \((p-1)/2\); and the two families meet only in the zero triple. Each root \(u_0\) of \(Q_k\) is an invariant of the scaling action, and the subsets realising it form a single orbit of \({\mathbb {F}}_p^{\times }\): if \(T\) has invariant \(u_0\ne 0\) and \(tT=T\) then \(t^{2}e_2=e_2\) and \(t^{3}e_3=e_3\), and \(e_2e_3\ne 0\) forces \(t^{2}=t^{3}=1\), hence \(t=1\). The action is therefore free and the orbit has exactly \(p-1\) elements, so \(u_0\) contributes \(p-1\) subsets when \(f_{u_0}\) splits into three distinct factors over \({\mathbb {F}}_p\) and none otherwise. This proves the displayed identity. For the criterion, one direction is immediate: if \(Q_k\) is constant the identity has only the two character terms. The other is not, and it is where the work is: if \(\deg Q_k{\gt}0\) then Proposition 13 and Lemma 14 show the fibre contribution is not PORC, so a fortiori it cannot be written in quadratic characters. For the list \(\{ 3,4,5,7\} \), the four monomials are \(s_3=3e_3\), \(s_4=2e_2^2\), \(s_5=-5e_2e_3\) and \(s_7=7e_2^2e_3\); that no other \(k\) joins them is not a computation but Proposition 15 below, which gives \(\deg Q_k\) in closed form for every \(k\) and shows it vanishes exactly there.

  • Program: the identity against exhaustive enumeration for 3 ≤ k ≤ 14 and primes 5 ≤ p ≤ 257 with p ∤ 6kD_k (620 pairs), with two failing controls. gates/P3d_columna_n3.py

Every value of \(6C_k(3,p)/(p-1)\) on the primes \(5\le p\le p_{\max }\), counted exactly (\(O(p)\) per prime: scaling acts freely on the triples), with \(\deg Q_k\) and whether \(e_2\), \(e_3\) divide \(s_k\).

The “only if” half of the criterion needs one further input, which we isolate rather than absorb into the proof below:

Proposition 13 an \(S_3\)-fibre exists
#

Uses

  • Lemma 21
📕 p. 14📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

If \(\deg Q_k{\gt}0\) then \(Q_k\) has a root \(u_0\) for which \(f_{u_0}(Y)=Y^3+u_0Y-u_0\) has Galois group \(S_3\) over \({\mathbb {Q}}(u_0)\).

🆕 Classical and new: unconditional, for every k (the paper’s card): the inequality A < 2^d for k ≥ 38 and forty printed certificates for 6 ≤ k ≤ 46.

↳ Used in: Theorem 12, Lemma 14

🛡️ Evidence & scope

  • Program: for 6 ≤ k ≤ 46 with d > 0: roots of Q_k real, positive and simple (Sturm), P_k irreducible modulo the printed prime (Table 3). gates/P3d_s3_certificados.py

  • Program: the raw leading coefficient 2 or k and A | k, by a separate route for 3 ≤ k ≤ 400. gates/P3d_lc_Qk.py

🧪 Lab: Figure 8 for your own k

Step one of Appendix A: \(s_k(\theta )=(-2\cos \theta )^k+2\cos k\theta \) on \((\pi /3,\pi /2)\), its sign changes between consecutive \(j\pi /k\), and the values \(u(\theta )\) they land on; the number of roots is compared with \(\deg Q_k\) and each \(u\) is checked as a root of \(Q_k\).

One \(S_3\) fibre is not by itself enough: the fibres are summed, and a reader is entitled to ask why the nonabelian contribution does not cancel against the others. It does not, and the reason is a permutation representation rather than an estimate.

Lemma 14 the nonabelian part cannot cancel
#

Uses

  • Proposition 13
  • Proposition 13
📕 p. 15📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

Let \(L/{\mathbb {Q}}\) be a finite Galois extension containing the roots of \(Q_k\) and of every \(f_{u_0}\) for \(u_0\) a root of \(Q_k\), and let \(G=\operatorname {Gal}(L/{\mathbb {Q}})\). Fix a \(G\)-orbit \(\mathcal O\) of roots of \(Q_k\), let \(H\) be the stabiliser of one of them, and let \(K=\ker \bigl(H\to S_3\bigr)\) for the action of \(H\) on the three roots of that fibre’s cubic. For \(p\) unramified in \(L\) and \(p\nmid 6k\mathfrak D_k\), let \(N_{\mathcal O}(p)\) be the number of roots of \(Q_k\) in \(\mathcal O\) that lie in \({\mathbb {F}}_p\) and whose cubic splits completely. Then

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle |H/K|\; N_{\mathcal O}(p)\; =\; \chi _{E[G/K]}(\operatorname {Frob}_p)}} , \qquad \text{so}\qquad 6\, N_{\mathcal O}(p)=\frac{6}{|H/K|}\, \chi _{E[G/K]}(\operatorname {Frob}_p) , \]

with \(E\) a splitting field for \(G\) as in (5), the factor \(6/|H/K|\) being a positive rational. If moreover \(H/K\simeq S_3\) — which Proposition 13 provides for some orbit, and where the factor is \(1\) — then \(E[G/K]\) has an irreducible constituent of dimension greater than one. Since the orbits enter Theorem 12 with coefficient \(+1\) each, that constituent cannot cancel, and \(C_k(3,p)\) is not PORC.

🆕 Classical and new: ours (the paper’s card).

↳ Used in: Theorem 12

Proof ▼

A coset \(gK\) is determined by the pair consisting of the root \(g(u_0)\in \mathcal O\) and the labelling of the three roots of \(f_{g(u_0)}\) induced by \(g\); the fibre of this correspondence over a root is \(H/K\), of size \(6\) exactly when \(H/K\simeq S_3\). Now \(\operatorname {Frob}_p\) fixes \(gK\) exactly when it fixes \(g(u_0)\) and acts trivially on the three roots of its cubic, that is, exactly when that root lies in \({\mathbb {F}}_p\) and its cubic splits completely. Each such root therefore contributes \(|H/K|\) fixed cosets and no other coset is fixed, which is the displayed identity, the character of a permutation representation being the number of fixed points.

For the second claim, \(H/K\) acts on the subset \(\{ hK\} \subseteq G/K\) by left translation, and that action is regular, so the image of \(G\) in \(\operatorname {Sym}(G/K)\) contains a subgroup isomorphic to \(H/K\simeq S_3\) and is not abelian. A representation all of whose irreducible constituents are one-dimensional has abelian image; hence \(E[G/K]\) has a constituent of dimension at least two. The coefficient field must be \(E\) and not \({\mathbb {Q}}\) here: over \(E\) every irreducible of an abelian group is one-dimensional, whereas over \({\mathbb {Q}}\) an abelian group can have irreducibles of larger dimension — already \({\mathbb {Q}}[C_3]={\mathbb {Q}}\times {\mathbb {Q}}(\zeta _3)\) has one of dimension two — so over \({\mathbb {Q}}\) the dimension alone would not exclude an abelian quotient. A PORC function is, by (5), one whose coefficients factor through an abelian quotient, and no such coefficient contains that constituent.

🛡️ Evidence & scope

  • Program: the identity 6N = χ_E[G/K](Frob_p) at k = 6 in 75 primes below 400, both sides computed independently, with a cyclic decoy. gates/P3d_caracter_regular_S3.py

[enhanced,sharp corners=downhill,boxrule=0.4pt,left=5pt,right=5pt, top=3pt,bottom=3pt,colback=fnuestro!4,colframe=fnuestro!55, fontupper=,before skip=6pt,after skip=8pt] fnuestroLemma 14fnuestroours
The lemma is the step from “some fibre has group \(S_3\)” to “the count is not PORC”. The intuition that a nonabelian fibre cannot be cancelled by the others is right, but turning it into a proof needs two things: the fibres organised as one permutation representation \(E[G/K]\), and the orbits entering with one sign, which is what Theorem 12 supplies. Nothing in the argument is deep, and the lemma is short.

Measured: The identity \(6N_{\mathcal O}(p)=\chi _{E[G/K]}(\operatorname {Frob}_p)\) in the case \(k=6\), where it can be checked and not merely argued: \(\deg Q_6=1\), its root \(3/2\) is rational, so \(H=G\), \(K=1\) and \(E[G/K]\) is the regular representation of \(S_3\) — a group already split by \(E={\mathbb {Q}}\), so that the check is a check over \({\mathbb {Q}}\). Both sides agree in all \(75\) primes \(5\le p{\lt}400\) with \(p\nmid 66\), with no exception, and neither is computed from the other: the left from a direct count of \(C_6(3,p)\) over \({\mathbb {F}}_p\), the right from the factorisation type of the cubic modulo \(p\). A decoy replacing the cubic by \(Y^3-3Y-1\), of square discriminant and cyclic group, correctly fails to support the argument. See gates/P3d_caracter_regular_S3.py.

[enhanced,sharp corners=downhill,boxrule=0.4pt,left=5pt,right=5pt, top=3pt,bottom=3pt,colback=fnuestro!4,colframe=fnuestro!55, fontupper=,before skip=6pt,after skip=8pt] fnuestroProposition 13fnuestrounconditional, for every \(k\)
The “only if” half of Theorem 12 is not immediate: it needs some fibre to have group \(S_3\), and that is a statement about \(Q_k\), not about the sieve. Appendix A proves it: all roots of \(Q_k\) real, positive and simple; no irreducible \(C_3\)-fibres; the divisibility \(\mathrm{lc}(Q_k)\mid k\), which is Waring’s formula read at the extreme monomial and gives \(A\le k\); the inequality \(A{\lt}2^{\deg Q_k}\), which \(A\le k\) secures for every \(k\) except the twenty-nine values \(k\le 37\) with \(\deg Q_k{\gt}0\) and \(k\ge 2^{\deg Q_k}\); and exact irreducibility certificates for \(P_k\) covering all \(6\le k\le 46\), which contains them. No step is left measured. The classification of Theorem 8 for \(n\ge 4\) does not depend on any of this.

Appendix A carries the proof in full, with its certificates; Section 8 says what about the family \(Q_k\) remains open, and it is not this. Measured: The identity checked against exhaustive enumeration for every \(3\le k\le 14\) and every prime \(5\le p\le 257\) with \(p\nmid 6k\mathfrak D_k\) — between \(50\) and \(53\) of the \(53\) primes in that range for each \(k\), \(620\) pairs \((k,p)\) in all — with no exception; replacing \(f_u\) by \(Y^3-uY-u\), or dropping the splitting condition, makes it fail. The factorisations of \(s_k\), the degree of \(Q_k\) and \(\mathfrak D_k\ne 0\) computed exactly for \(k\le 30\). Note in particular \(C_7(3,p)=(p-1)(4+\chi _p(-3))/6\), the same closed form as \(C_5(3,p)\). See gates/P3d_columna_n3.py.

[enhanced,sharp corners=downhill,boxrule=0.4pt,left=5pt,right=5pt, top=3pt,bottom=3pt,colback=fnuestro!4,colframe=fnuestro!55, fontupper=,before skip=6pt,after skip=8pt] fnuestroTheorem 12fnuestroours — the count, not the polynomials
The polynomials and the reduction to \(u\) are Helou’s  [ 16 ] and are cited above. What is stated here is arithmetic over \({\mathbb {F}}_p\): that the subset count decomposes with no remainder into the two character families and one term of size \(p-1\) per split fibre, and that it is expressible in quadratic characters exactly when \(Q_k\) is constant. That question is not the one [ 16 , 41 , 33 ] ask — they work over \({\mathbb {Q}}\) and towards Fermat — and the list \(\{ 3,4,5,7\} \) is the answer to ours.

Figure 5 is that measurement rather than the statement: it shows every value the count takes, and the decomposition can be read off it directly — the elementary \(k\) occupy one or two levels, and every other \(k\) climbs in steps of six, one step per root of \(Q_k\) whose cubic splits.

The list \(\{ 3,4,5,7\} \) looks accidental. It is not: it is the zero set of a formula.

🖼️ Figure 5

Theorem 12 measured rather than stated: every value \(6C_k(3,p)/(p-1)\) takes on the \(53\) primes \(p\le 257\) (omitting \(p\mid k\)), with the area of each disc the share of primes giving it and the count printed for the rare ones. The green columns are the four elementary \(k\); everywhere else the values climb in steps of \(6\), one step per root of \(Q_k\) whose cubic splits, on top of the \(0\) or \(2\) contributed by \(e_2\) and the \(3\) contributed by \(e_3\).

Proposition 15 the degree of \(Q_k\)
#

Lean declarations

  • P3d.card_degreePairs
  • P3d.card_degreePairs_eq_one_iff
📕 p. 16📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

For every \(k\ge 3\),

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle \deg Q_k=\Bigl\lfloor \frac k6\Bigr\rfloor -\bigl[\, k\equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ 6)\, \bigr]}} . \]

In particular \(\deg Q_k=0\) exactly for \(k\in \{ 3,4,5,7\} \), and since the degree is nondecreasing along each residue class modulo \(6\), no further \(k\) can return to zero.

Proof: in this note·Covers: not formalized·Cite: Lemma 1, p. 4, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22886543

🆕 Classical and new: for odd k the number is Helou’s r_k [Helou]; the paper claims neither, only a self-contained proof for all k.

↳ Used in: Theorem 12

Proof ▼

Newton–Waring at \(e_1=0\) is (9) below, and no coefficient there vanishes, so the monomials of \(s_k\) are exactly the pairs \((a,b)\ge 0\) with \(2a+3b=k\). Those pairs form a chain: \(b\) runs over the integers with \(b\equiv k\pmod2\) and \(0\le b\le k/3\), and \(a\) is determined. Dividing out the common monomial leaves consecutive powers of \(u=e_2^3/e_3^2\), whence

\[ \deg Q_k=\# \bigl\{ (a,b)\ge 0:\ 2a+3b=k\bigr\} -1 . \]

Counting the admissible \(b\) gives \(\lfloor k/6\rfloor +1\) in every residue class except \(k\equiv 1\pmod6\), where the parity constraint costs one, and subtracting \(1\) is the formula.

🛡️ Evidence & scope

  • Program: both sides independently for 3 ≤ k ≤ 90, and every proper factor of s_k homogeneous in u. gates/P3d_grado_Qk.py

🧪 Lab: Figure 6: deg Q_k read off s_k

For every \(k\le k_{\max }\): \(s_k\) in \(e_2,e_3\) by \(s_k=-e_2s_{k-2}+e_3s_{k-3}\), its factors \(e_2\), \(e_3\) removed, as a polynomial in \(u=e_2^3/e_3^2\); its degree against \(\lfloor k/6\rfloor -[k\equiv 1 \bmod 6]\) (Proposition 15) and against \(\dim M_{2k}(\mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbf Z))-1\) (Proposition 16).

The six residue classes give six ladders of slope \(1/6\), one of which — and only one, the class of \(k\equiv 1\) — starts a step below the others; Figure 6 is the statement drawn. The exceptional class is the whole of the irregularity, and it is what makes \(7\) join \(3,4,5\): without it the elementary \(k\) would be \(\{ 3,4,5\} \) and the column would look like the trichotomy of Section 2, which it does not.

🖼️ Figure 6

Proposition 15. The grey line is \(k/6\). What the picture adds to the formula is that the exceptional class is a single ladder rather than a scatter of exceptions, and that the four circled points are the only ones that will ever touch zero.

Two computational facts about the family are worth recording, because the criterion of Theorem 12 is only useful if \(Q_k\) can be produced. Specialising the Newton–Waring formula to \(e_1=0\) gives

\begin{equation} \tag {9} s_k\; =\; k\sum _{\substack {a,b\ge 0\\ 2a+3b=k}}(-1)^{a}\, \frac{(a+b-1)!}{a!\, b!}\; e_2^{a}e_3^{b}, \end{equation}
15

in which no coefficient vanishes. And writing \(R_k(u)=u^{-\lceil k/3\rceil }s_k(u,u)\), so that \(R_k\) is \(Q_k\) up to the integer content, one has the two recursions

\[ R_k=R_{k-3}-u^{\, [\, 3\mid k\, ]}R_{k-2}, \qquad R_{k+18}=(3-2u)R_{k+12}-(u^{2}+6u+3)R_{k+6}+R_k . \]

The second has coefficients independent of \(k\) and order three, which is what one should expect: if \(y_1,y_2,y_3\) are the roots of \(Y^3+uY-u\), the three numbers \(\beta _i=y_i^{6}/u^{2}\) have elementary symmetric functions \(3-2u\), \(u^2+6u+3\) and \(1\), and \(R_{k+6}\) is the corresponding power sum. There is no reason to look for a two-term Chebyshev-like relation.

Measured: (9) against the recursion for \(2\le k\le 60\); both recursions verified symbolically, the first for \(3\le k{\lt}40\) and the second for \(0\le k\le 21\); and the three symmetric functions of the \(\beta _i\) computed from the power sums \(s_6\) and \(s_{12}\) without extracting roots. See gates/P3d_familia_Qk.py.

Proposition 16 the degree is a dimension of modular forms
#
📕 p. 18📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

Substitute \(e_2=-3E_4\) and \(e_3=2E_6\), with \(E_4,E_6\) the normalised Eisenstein series. Then \(\mathcal F_k=s_k(-3E_4,2E_6)\) is a modular form of weight \(2k\) for \(\mathrm{SL}_2({\mathbb {Z}})\), and since \(M_*(\mathrm{SL}_2({\mathbb {Z}}))=\mathbf C[E_4,E_6]\) a basis of \(M_{2k}\) is indexed by the solutions of \(2a+3b=k\) — the same set that indexes the terms of \(s_k\). Hence

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle \dim M_{2k}=\deg Q_k+1}}, \]

and \(\dim M_{2k}=1\) exactly for \(k\in \{ 3,4,5,7\} \).

This is what makes the exceptional class conceptual rather than accidental. The four weights are \(6,8,10,14\), and the corresponding forms are \(E_6\), \(E_8\), \(E_{10}\), \(E_{14}\): weight \(14\) is still one-dimensional after weight \(12\) has reached dimension two, because that is where the first cusp form \(\Delta \) appears. The class \(k\equiv 1\pmod6\) is one step behind the others in the degree for the same reason that \(\dim M_{2k}\) lags there. Normalising by the constant term \(2^k+2(-1)^k\) gives those four Eisenstein series on the nose; already for \(k=6\) the form is not Eisenstein, since \(\mathcal F_6/66=(9E_4^3+2E_6^2)/11\), and \(Q_k\) records the zeros of \(\mathcal F_k\) that survive after the elliptic points are removed.

Corollary 17 the criterion is a dimension

For every \(k\ge 3\),

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle C_k(3,p)\ \text{is elementary} \iff \dim M_{2k}(\mathrm{SL}_2({\mathbb {Z}}))=1 .}} \]

Proof: in this note·Covers: not formalized·Cite: Corollary 17, p. 18, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22886543

🆕 Classical and new: ours — but only the joining of two halves (the paper’s card).

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

Proof ▼

By Theorem 12, \(C_k(3,p)\) is elementary if and only if \(\deg Q_k=0\), and by Proposition 16 that is \(\dim M_{2k}=1\). The one-dimensional weights are \(2k\in \{ 4,6,8,10,14\} \), and \(2k=4\) is excluded by \(k\ge 3\); the remaining four are the list of Theorem 12.

[enhanced,sharp corners=downhill,boxrule=0.4pt,left=5pt,right=5pt, top=3pt,bottom=3pt,colback=fnuestro!4,colframe=fnuestro!55, fontupper=,before skip=6pt,after skip=8pt] fnuestroCorollary 17fnuestroours — but only the joining of two halves
Neither half is new here: the criterion \(\deg Q_k=0\) is Theorem 12 and the dimension formula is classical. What the corollary contributes is that they are the same condition, which is what turns an arbitrary-looking list into one sentence. The proof is three lines and the content is the identification, not the argument.

Measured: \(\dim M_{2k}=\deg Q_k+1\) for \(3\le k\le 60\), against the degrees computed by factoring \(s_k\), and \(\dim M_{2k}=1\) exactly on \(\{ 2,3,4,5,7\} \) for \(k{\lt}200\) — with \(k=2\) outside the range \(k\ge 3\) of this note, which is why the corollary’s list has four entries and not five. See gates/P3d_familia_Qk.py.

That is the statement to remember. The list \(\{ 3,4,5,7\} \) looks arbitrary and is not: it is the one-dimensional weights \(6,8,10,14\), read through a sieve over \({\mathbb {F}}_p\). The reason \(6\) drops out and \(7\) comes back is the cusp forms: \(S_w=\Delta \, M_{w-12}\), so \(\dim M_{12}=2\) because \(\Delta \) itself is there, while \(S_{14}=\Delta M_2=0\) because \(M_2=0\) — and weight \(14\) is one-dimensional again. It is the gap above the first cusp form, not a position below it.

The structure \(M_*=\mathbf C[E_4,E_6]\) and the resulting basis of \(M_{2k}\) are classical; see for instance  [ 28 , Prop. 4.16 ] . What is used here is only the coincidence of index sets, and the consequence for \(\deg Q_k\) follows from Proposition 15.

Measured: Both sides computed independently for \(3\le k\le 90\) — the left by factoring \(s_k\) in \({\mathbb {Z}}[e_2,e_3]\) and reading the degree in \(u\), the right by the formula — with no discrepancy; and every proper factor of \(s_k\) verified to be homogeneous in \(u\) over the same range. See gates/P3d_grado_Qk.py.

[enhanced,sharp corners=downhill,boxrule=0.4pt,left=5pt,right=5pt, top=3pt,bottom=3pt,colback=fajeno!4,colframe=fajeno!55, fontupper=,before skip=6pt,after skip=8pt] fajenoProposition 15fajenothe number is Helou’s; the proof above is self-contained
For odd \(k\) this degree is Helou’s \(r_k=(k-3-2b)/6\)  [ 16 ] , with \(b\) as in Section 6, restated in  [ 41 , § 2 ] , and our closed form \(\lfloor k/6\rfloor -[k\equiv 1]\) is the same number written differently; for even \(k\) it is the construction that  [ 34 , § 5.4 ] states can be carried out. We claim neither. What the proof above adds is only that it needs neither: counting the solutions of \(2a+3b=k\) settles all \(k\) at once, which matters because Theorem 12 rests on the consequence — the degree is monotone along each residue class, so no \(k\) beyond \(\{ 3,4,5,7\} \) can return to zero.

Theorem 12 also settles the two shades of Figure 1. Call the group of the class function the smallest finite quotient of \(G_{\mathbb {Q}}\) through which the class function above factors. A sufficient criterion for it to be exactly \(S_3\) is that two things hold at once: \(Q_k\) has a single rational root, so that there is one fibre and it is defined over \({\mathbb {Q}}\); and \(e_2\nmid s_k\), so that the count does not also carry \(\chi _p(-3)\). We do not claim the criterion is necessary for every \(k\). The second condition is not by itself enough to force \(S_3\times C_2\), and the missing step is arithmetic rather than formal: the quadratic subfield of the fibre cubic’s splitting field is generated by \(\sqrt{\operatorname {disc}f_{u_0}}\), and it coincides with \({\mathbb {Q}}(\sqrt{-3})\) exactly when that discriminant is \(-3\) times a square. It never does here — for \(k=8,10,11,13\) the squarefree parts are \(-43,-57,-31,-35\) — so the two fields are distinct, the compositum has degree twelve, and the group is \(S_3\times C_2\). In the range of Figure 1 the computation shows that the criterion is met exactly for \(k=6,9\), and those are the cells drawn darker.

Measured: For \(3\le k\le 14\): the degree of \(Q_k\), the rationality of its roots, whether \(e_2\mid s_k\), the discriminant of the fibre cubic and its squarefree part, each computed separately; the four discriminants above are checked not to be \(-3\) times a square, with a control showing the check can see the case where one is. See gates/P3d_grupo_del_caracter.py.

Remark 18 what the column is really counting
#
📕 p. 19📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

Normalise the cubic attached to a root \(u\) of \(Q_k\) as \(f_u(Y)=Y^3+uY-u\), with \(\operatorname {disc}(f_u)=-u^{2}(4u+27)\), and let \(E_u\) be the elliptic curve \(V^2=f_u(Y)\), of \(j\)-invariant \(6912u/(4u+27)\). Then

\[ { \boxed {\displaystyle f_u\ \text{splits completely over }{\mathbb {F}}_p \iff E_u[2]\subseteq E_u({\mathbb {F}}_p)}} , \]

because \(S_3=\mathrm{GL}_2({\mathbb {F}}_2)\) acting on the three nonzero \(2\)-torsion points is exactly the Galois action on the roots. So at \(n=3\) the count is of fibres with fully rational \(2\)-torsion, over a finite set of values of the modular parameter. This resolves what looks like a paradox in Observation 20: there are elliptic curves behind the zero-dimensional problem too, but what is counted there is their torsion, which takes finitely many states, and not their trace.

Measured: \(\operatorname {disc}(Y^3+uY-u)=-u^2(4u+27)\) and, for \(k=11\), \(u=1\) giving \(Y^3+Y-1\) of discriminant \(-31\) and Galois group \(S_3\). See gates/P3d_familia_Qk.py.

Remark 19 a null that a short window would have manufactured
#
📕 p. 20📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

For \(k=9\) one has \(s_9=-3e_3(3e_2^3-e_3^2)\), so the count should take two values. Over the \(14\) primes \(5\le p\le 53\) it takes one: the second family first appears at \(p=71\), and then at \(83,97,131,193,257\). A family of Chebotarev density \(1/6\) is expected about twice in fourteen primes, so its absence there is not evidence of absence. We record this because the criterion is general: a null result on a window too short to see the predicted density is not a null result.

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

So under the narrow reading — coefficients in quadratic characters of fixed integers — even \(n=3\) stops being elementary at \(k=6\); under the broad reading, arbitrary Artin-type class functions, \(n=3\) is elementary for every \(k\). The classification of Theorem 8 is stated for the broad reading, and Figure 1 keeps the two apart by colour. The distinction is not a blemish: it is the reason the two halves of this note fail to be PORC — polynomial on residue classes, in Higman’s sense  [ 10 ] — for structurally different reasons.

Observation 20 the two failures are not the same failure; cf.  [ 17 ]
#

Uses

  • Theorem 8
📕 p. 20📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

At \(n=3\), \(k=6\) the count takes exactly two polynomial values, \(p-1\) and \(0\), and the partition of the primes between them is a splitting condition in a nonabelian extension — the class function is the indicator of a conjugacy class, not a character. It is therefore not PORC but it is polynomial on Frobenius sets, POFS in the sense of Stanojkovski–Voll  [ 47 , § 1.5.2 ] . For \(n\ge 4\) the surviving object is the Frobenius trace of a curve of positive genus, and the count is not POFS either — not because of how many values it takes, but because a POFS function is Artin–Tate in the sense of (5) and Theorem 8 rules that out by weight one. The two failures are therefore separated by weight, and the numerical growth of the set of values is an illustration of the difference rather than the argument for it. The archetype usually offered for the first mode is du Sautoy–Vaughan-Lee  [ 5 ] , whose non-PORC behaviour is likewise a finite-valued count partitioned by a nonabelian splitting condition rather than a surviving trace; Isham’s separation  [ 17 , § 2.4.2 ] is the one that already contains both.

↳ Not used by another result of the paper.

Measured: For \(n=3\), \(k=6\): exactly two values across all \(p\le 2000\) with \(p\nmid 66\), and no modulus among \(4,6,8,12,24,33,36,44,66,72,99,132,264,396\) and \(1188\) — the last being the discriminant itself — assigns a single value to every residue class. For \(n=5\), \(k=3\): the number of distinct Frobenius traces of the conductor-\(20\) curve grows \(15\to 24\to 31\to 52\) as the window grows \(p\le 200,500,1000,2000\) (\(p\nmid 20\)), while the control quantity \(\chi _p(-3)\) takes two values on the same window. Four windows fix no exponent and none is claimed: one quantity is bounded by a theorem, while the observed support of the other keeps growing across these windows, and that is the distinction Observation 20 draws. See gates/P3b_pofs_vs_porc.py.

Figure 7 puts the two measurements on one page, which is the only place in this note where the two failures can be compared directly rather than described in turn.
