The “not POFS” conclusion comes from weight one and not from this numerical growth: one quantity is bounded by a theorem, while the observed support of the other keeps growing across these windows. A reader who wants a single picture of why “not PORC” is too coarse a verdict for this classification should look at these two panels together.

[enhanced,sharp corners=downhill,boxrule=0.4pt,left=5pt,right=5pt, top=3pt,bottom=3pt,colback=fajeno!4,colframe=fajeno!55, fontupper=,before skip=6pt,after skip=8pt] fajenoObservation 20fajenonot ours — Isham has it
The coexistence of the two modes in one classification, and their separation by the size of the contribution, is already in Isham  [ 17 , § § 2.3.3, 2.4.2 ] : her Example 2.3.8 isolates a zero-dimensional stratum \(z^3-z-1\) with Galois group \(S_3\) and notes that a nonabelian group makes the count nonquasipolynomial, her Proposition 2.3.7 bounds all such strata by a constant independent of \(q\), and §2.4.2 contrasts that \(O(1)\) with a Frobenius trace equidistributed on \([-2\sqrt p,2\sqrt p]\). It is the engine of her proof, not a remark. What is not in that treatment is the positive half — that the bounded mode is still POFS in the sense of  [ 47 , § 1.5.2 ] — and that is all we add here.

7 Where this sits

Almost every ingredient of this note belongs to someone else, and the list is long enough to be worth reading as one: the polynomial family and its \(S_3\) reduction to Cauchy and Liouville in 1839, Mirimanoff in 1903 and Helou in 1997; the criterion for four roots of unity to Mann in 1965; the vanishing of \(H^1\) in higher dimension to Ghorpade and Lachaud; the sieve to Li and Wan; the triples of Remark 10 to Sziklai and Takáts in 2008; the coexistence of the two failure modes to Isham in 2021; and the vocabulary for that coexistence to Stanojkovski and Voll. What is left is a single question about counting over \({\mathbb {F}}_p\), and it is worth asking why so small a residue survives so much company.

The answer is not that nobody looked. It is that the neighbouring literature mostly cannot state the question in its own language. The exact evaluation frameworks that include the first moment — the Vandermonde sets of  [ 45 , 22 ] and the consecutive pair of  [ 36 , 35 ] — prescribe an initial segment \(s_1=\dots =s_m=0\); so does the decision problem of  [ 18 ] , which is discussed below and which bounds rather than evaluates. Two frameworks are more general in the index set, and both stop short in a different way: they do not evaluate in the regime \(d_1=1\) that our pairs live in, \(d_1\) being the smallest prescribed exponent in the notation of  [ 15 ] . Giménez, Matera, Pérez and Privitelli  [ 14 ] allow an arbitrary index set \(I=\{ i_1{\lt}\dots {\lt}i_m\} \) subject to \(i_m\le n-3\), which includes our \(I=\{ 1,k\} \) exactly in the range \(k\le n-3\), and Gottig, Pérez and Privitelli  [ 15 ] allow non-consecutive exponents; both obtain bounds for each factorisation pattern — bounds, not an evaluation, and it is the evaluation that the gap between the indices governs. The hypothesis \(2\le d_1\) of  [ 15 ] excludes the first moment outright. For the Vandermonde sets the initial segment is not a convention but the definition: the invariant \(w_T\) is the first non-vanishing moment, so a set with \(s_1=s_6=0\) and \(s_2\ne 0\) is simply not a Vandermonde set of any kind, and at \(p=19\) that is every one of the eighteen triples. The gap between the two prescribed indices is invisible there by construction.

And the gap is where the arithmetic is. With consecutive indices the conditions become a congruence in a truncated unit group and the character sums are Gauss sums of known value — that is exactly why  [ 36 , 35 ] close the case \(\{ 1,2\} \) for every subset size. Leave one index out and the coset structure goes with it: \(s_1=s_3=0\) forces \(e_1=e_3=0\) with \(e_2\) free, the length-four strata become plane curves, and a Frobenius trace can survive. The classification of this note is, in that light, a map of where the gap bites.

The consecutive pair \(\{ 1,2\} \) over \({\mathbb {F}}_q\) with both moments zero is settled, and settled for every subset size: Nguyen  [ 36 , Thm. 2.11 ] and Zhang, Zheng, Wang and Yuan  [ 35 , Cor. 21 ] evaluate every Li–Wan stratum in closed form, uniformly in the subset size \(n\) — the pair of exponents there is fixed at \(\{ 1,2\} \), so the uniformity is in \(n\) and not in our second exponent \(k\). The reason that works is structural and it is exactly the reason it does not transfer. The pair \(\{ 1,2\} \) makes the conditions a congruence \(\prod _i(1+x_iy)\equiv 1\pmod{y^3}\), a coset in a truncated unit group whose characters are quadratic Gauss sums with known exact values; weight one is present but it is never unknown. Our pair \(\{ 1,3\} \) gives \(e_1=e_3=0\) with \(e_2\) free, which is not a congruence of that shape, and the length-four strata are plane curves whose traces are not determined by anything smaller. The first non-consecutive pair is where an unknown Frobenius trace can appear, and Theorem 8 says exactly when it does.

On the decision side, Lai–Marino–Robinson–Wan  [ 18 ] decide positivity of the consecutive \(m\)-th moment subset count in polynomial time for fixed \(m\); they use the same Li–Wan sieve, but to bound each stratum by \(((mn+1)\sqrt q)^{e_i}\), and the distinction our classification turns on is precisely what such a bound discards. Their framework reaches the index set \(\{ 1,3\} \) in one place only: they may drop the moments with \(p\mid j\), and dropping \(j=2\) while keeping \(1\) and \(3\) requires \(p=2\). That is the characteristic in which Moisio and Ranto  [ 27 ] found the same index pair producing elliptic curves for the opposite factorisation type — a second independent arrival at \(\{ 1,3\} \) in characteristic two, and a third in all, by a route that meets neither of the others.

Exact counts for systems of two diagonal equations exist in a few families — Cao–Chou–Gu  [ 11 ] for \(\sum X_i=\sum X_i^{p^\ell +1}=0\) over \({\mathbb {F}}_{p^{2\ell t}}\), and Castro–Rubio–Guan–Figueroa  [ 12 ] for the Waring number of the same exponent family — but these count tuples rather than subsets of distinct elements, which is the condition that produces the partition sieve in the first place, and their exponent is tied to the characteristic: \(p^\ell +1=3\) forces \(p=2\), so the fixed exponent \(3\) over an odd prime field is not reachable there. Gottig–Pérez–Privitelli, besides the hypothesis \(2\le d_1\) already noted, work with unit coefficients rather than the repeated weights (1) produces.

Finally, the shape of this story is not new even if the object is. Kontsevich conjectured that graph hypersurfaces have (quasi-)polynomial point counts; Stembridge  [ 46 ] verified it for small graphs, Belkale and Brosnan  [ 1 ] disproved it in general, and Brown and Schnetz  [ 3 ] exhibited explicit counterexamples whose counting functions involve a modular form of a singular K3 surface. Closed forms in the small cases, and a surviving motive after them, is a recurring pattern; what varies is the weight at which the survival happens. Here it is weight one, which is why at \(k=3\), \(n=5\) an elliptic curve and not a modular form of higher weight is what one meets; at \(k=5\), \(n=6\) it is the genus-five curve of Section 8.

One last observation belongs here rather than in the appendix, because it is about the object and not about the people. The identity behind the family \(E_k\) is not the subject of the 1839 paper that contains it: it appears inside a referee report, found by Liouville and Cauchy while checking Lamé’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem for the exponent seven, and judged by them “assez curieux pour mériter d’être indiqué dans ce rapport”  [ 13 ] . The polynomial extracted in passing while auditing someone else’s argument is still, a hundred and eighty years later, the one whose irreducibility nobody can settle — and the one our criterion evaluates. Appendix B tells that story, and the others of Figure 2, in full.

Code and data availability

Every computational claim marked Measured names a script, and the scripts are not internal paths: the verification code and the data behind every figure and table in this note are archived with it, at doi:10.5281/zenodo.22886542, so that each gates/… reference resolves to a file a reader can run. Nothing in the note depends on a computation that is only described. The scripts need Python with sympy and numpy; the certificates of Table 3 need neither, since each row is one irreducibility check modulo one printed prime and is verifiable in any computer algebra system.

8 What is left open

The family \(Q_k\): what is open there is not ours either. The irreducibility of \(E_k\) over \({\mathbb {Q}}\) for \(k\) prime is Mirimanoff’s conjecture  [ 32 ] , still open; Helou  [ 16 , Prop. 2 ] shows it is equivalent to the irreducibility of \(T_k\), so it is a question about exactly the polynomial our criterion evaluates, and  [ 20 ] is the current state of it. A closed coefficient formula is already known  [ 34 , (4.4) ] . The exceptional class \(k\equiv 1\pmod6\), which looked accidental, is explained by Proposition 16: it is where \(\dim M_{2k}\) lags, and the lag is the appearance of \(\Delta \) in weight \(12\). What remains genuinely open is the arithmetic of the \(Q_k\) that our criterion evaluates, and there the question is Mirimanoff’s, not ours.

Proposition 13 is proved, and the proof is in Appendix A. It is stated here because Proposition 13, with Lemma 14, gives that \(k\ge 6\) and \(k\ne 7\) imply \(C_k(3,p)\) is not PORC, which is what closes the “only if” half of Theorem 12; what remains open about the family \(Q_k\) is Mirimanoff’s question above, not ours.

The Jacobian of the genus-five curve of \(k=5\), \(n=6\), is not \({\mathbb {Q}}\)-simple. It decomposes: writing \(w=x_1\), \(a=x_2+w\), \(b=x_3+w\), \(c=x_4+w\) and \(A=ab+ac+bc\), so that \(a+b+c=0\), the quintic \(C\) becomes \((6w^2-A)B+2wA(2w^2-A)=0\) with \(B=abc\), since \(3w^5+\sum (a-w)^5=5\bigl[(6w^2-A)B+2wA(2w^2-A)\bigr]\). Write \(\widetilde C\) for its normalisation. The quotient of \(\widetilde C\) by \(S_3\) is a rational curve, and \(\widetilde C\) is the Galois closure of a cubic over it. Quotienting by \(A_3\) gives the elliptic curve \(E_0\colon v^2=x^3-147x-718\), of \(j\)-invariant \(-235298/13\); quotienting by a transposition gives the genus-two curve \(D\colon v^2=t^6+12t^4+40t^3+36t^2+48t+16\), whose sextic has discriminant \(2^{35}3^{6}\cdot 13\). The idempotent relations of Kani and Rosen  [ 19 ] then give \(J(\widetilde C)\sim _{{\mathbb {Q}}}E_0\times J(D)^2\), so \(a_p(\widetilde C)=a_p(E_0)+2a_p(D)\); that step is quoted, not certified here.

What we do certify is that the genus-two factor does not decompose further, and the certificate is two primes, an irreducibility certificate at each, and four comparisons of integers at each. At \(p=11\) and \(p=19\) the curve \(D\) has \(11\) and \(25\) points over \({\mathbb {F}}_p\), and \(111\) and \(373\) over \({\mathbb {F}}_{p^2}\). Since \(\# D({\mathbb {F}}_p)=p+1+a_1\) and \(\# D({\mathbb {F}}_{p^2})=p^2+1-a_1^2+2a_2\), the first count fixes \(a_1\) and only the second fixes \(a_2\); together they give the Weil polynomials \(T^4+a_1T^3+a_2T^2+a_1pT+p^2\), namely

\[ T^4-T^3-5T^2-11T+121 , \qquad T^4+5T^3+18T^2+95T+361 , \]

with \((a_1,a_2)=(-1,-5)\) and \((5,18)\). Both come with a certificate of the same kind as Table 3: the first polynomial is already irreducible modulo \(2\), the second modulo \(17\), which proves each irreducible over \({\mathbb {Q}}\) in one line, so \(J(D)\) is simple at both primes. Both reductions are ordinary, since \(p\nmid a_2\) in each. For a simple ordinary abelian surface, Howe and Zhu  [ 9 , Thm. 6 ] show that absolute simplicity fails in exactly four cases — \(a_1=0\), \(a_1^2=p+a_2\), \(a_1^2=2a_2\) and \(a_1^2=3a_2-3p\), splitting over an extension of degree \(2\), \(3\), \(4\) and \(6\) respectively — and neither of ours is one:

\[ 1\notin \{ 6,\, -10,\, -48\} , \qquad 25\notin \{ 37,\, 36,\, -3\} , \]

with \(a_1\ne 0\) both times. So the reduction of \(J(D)\) is absolutely simple at both primes, and therefore so is \(J(D)\) over \(\overline{\mathbb {Q}}\): a proper abelian subvariety, defined over some number field, would reduce at a prime of good reduction to a proper abelian subvariety of the reduction. Nothing here is decided numerically.

Absolute simplicity alone does not give \(\mathrm{End}^0_{\overline{\mathbb {Q}}}J(D)={\mathbb {Q}}\). By Albert’s classification, the endomorphism algebra of a simple abelian surface is \({\mathbb {Q}}\), a real quadratic field, a quartic CM field or an indefinite quaternion algebra over \({\mathbb {Q}}\)  [ 2 ] , and each of the last three contains a real quadratic field \(F\). The bridge to the finite fields is specialisation. The endomorphisms of \(J(D)\) are all defined over some number field \(K'\), and at a prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(K'\) above a prime \(p\) of good reduction, reduction of endomorphisms is an injective ring homomorphism \(\operatorname {End}_{K'} J(D)\hookrightarrow \operatorname {End}_{{\mathbb {F}}_{\mathfrak p}}(J(D)\bmod \mathfrak p)\); tensoring with \({\mathbb {Q}}\), \(\mathrm{End}^0_{\overline{\mathbb {Q}}}J(D)\) embeds in \(\mathrm{End}^0_{\overline{\mathbb {F}}_p}(J(D)\bmod p)\). At \(p=11\) and \(p=19\) the reduction is ordinary and, as just shown, absolutely simple. Over \({\mathbb {F}}_{p^m}\) its endomorphism algebra is, by Tate  [ 39 ] and in the ordinary case Waterhouse  [ 40 ] , commutative and equal to the Frobenius field \({\mathbb {Q}}(\alpha ^m)\), \(\alpha \) a root of the Weil polynomial at \(p\); and absolute simplicity gives \({\mathbb {Q}}(\alpha ^m)={\mathbb {Q}}(\alpha )\) for every \(m\), so the algebra does not grow with the base field and the geometric algebra \(\mathrm{End}^0_{\overline{\mathbb {F}}_p}\) is the quartic CM field \({\mathbb {Q}}(\alpha )\). Hence \(F\) would embed in \({\mathbb {Q}}(\alpha )\) at both primes. Those fields are quartic CM, and the real quadratic subfield of each is read off the resolvent \(T^2+a_1T+(a_2-2p)\) satisfied by \(\alpha +p/\alpha \): here \(T^2-T-27\) and \(T^2+5T-20\), of discriminants \(109\) and \(105\), both squarefree. The subfields are therefore \({\mathbb {Q}}(\sqrt{109})\) and \({\mathbb {Q}}(\sqrt{105})\) — distinct, so the two quartic fields are not even isomorphic, and nothing but \({\mathbb {Q}}\) survives. What is not done is assembling this into a formula for \(C_5(6,p)\): the other strata, including those of higher dimension, still have to be treated.

Measured: \(j(E_0)=-235298/13\); the sextic discriminant \(2^{35}3^{6}\cdot 13\); and \(\# D({\mathbb {F}}_{11})=11\), \(\# D({\mathbb {F}}_{19})=25\), \(\# D({\mathbb {F}}_{121})=111\) and \(\# D({\mathbb {F}}_{361})=373\), by direct enumeration, against the stated Weil polynomials, including their functional equation; and a control showing that the count over \({\mathbb {F}}_p\) alone leaves dozens of values of \(a_2\) open. Separately, the two certificates of irreducibility — modulo \(2\) and modulo \(17\) — and the four Howe–Zhu comparisons at each prime, all in integer arithmetic. Two decoys, each aimed at one half of the argument: for absolute simplicity, the Weil restriction \(T^4-T^2+121\) at \(p=11\), which is irreducible over \({\mathbb {Q}}\) like ours but meets condition \(a_1=0\) and splits over \({\mathbb {F}}_{p^2}\), where its Weil polynomial becomes \((T^2-T+121)^2\); and for the endomorphism step, a curve with complex multiplication, \(v^2=t^5-1\), whose two Frobenius fields give the same real subfield \({\mathbb {Q}}(\sqrt5)\), so the criterion correctly declines to certify it. See gates/P3d_weil_D.py, gates/P3d_familia_Qk.py and gates/P3d_jacobiana_genero5.py.

The counting function of the non-elementary cases. Theorem 8 says what \(C_k(n,p)\) is not. For \(k=3\), \(n=5\) the companion note says what it is, in terms of one elliptic curve. For \(k=5\), \(n=6\) the obstruction is the genus-five curve whose Jacobian is decomposed above as \(E_0\times J(D)^{2}\); what is missing there is not the curve but the assembly, since the other strata — including those of higher dimension — still have to be treated.

Whether weight one is the only obstruction. Remark 7 shows that a higher stratum can carry non-Artin–Tate \(H^2\) while its \(H^1\) vanishes. Our method cannot see that, so for the cases it declares Artin–Tate the proof is always by exhibiting a formula. A criterion that sees all weights at once would subsume both halves of this note.

A Proof of Proposition 13

What is proved here. Proposition 13: whenever \(\deg Q_k{\gt}0\), some fibre \(f_{u_0}\) has Galois group \(S_3\) over \({\mathbb {Q}}(u_0)\). Combined with Lemma 14, this is what Theorem 12 needs: \(k\ge 6\) and \(k\ne 7\) imply \(C_k(3,p)\) is not PORC — and the exclusion of \(7\) is not a technicality, it is forced by Theorem 12, which gives \(C_7(3,p)\) in quadratic characters, so any statement covering \(k\ge 6\) without qualification has its counterexample printed in this same note.

The proof runs in four steps.

Step one: the roots of \(Q_k\) are real, positive and simple. One parametrisation makes the whole step visible. A triple summing to zero with two roots on the unit circle is

\[ (x,y,z)=\bigl(e^{i\theta },\, e^{-i\theta },\, -2\cos \theta \bigr), \]

and then \(e_2=1-4\cos ^{2}\theta \), \(e_3=-2\cos \theta \), so that

\begin{equation} \tag {10} { \boxed {\displaystyle u(\theta )=\frac{(1-4\cos ^{2}\theta )^{3}}{4\cos ^{2}\theta }}}, \qquad s_k=(-2\cos \theta )^{k}+2\cos k\theta . \end{equation}
16

On \(\pi /3{\lt}\theta {\lt}\pi /2\) the numerator and denominator are both positive and \(u\) increases monotonically from \(0\) to \(\infty \), so every positive real value of the invariant is attained exactly once on that interval, and the roots of \(Q_k\) correspond to the zeros of \(s_k\) there. Those are located by the sign alternation of \((-2\cos \theta )^k+2\cos k\theta \) at \(\theta =j\pi /k\) for \(\lceil k/3\rceil \le j\le \lfloor k/2\rfloor \). The number of sign changes is the number of such \(j\) minus one, and that number is the degree itself:

\[ \# \{ \text{sign changes}\} =\Bigl\lfloor \frac k2\Bigr\rfloor -\Bigl\lceil \frac k3\Bigr\rceil =\deg Q_k=:d . \]

So the changes produce \(d\) distinct real positive roots, and since \(Q_k\) has degree exactly \(d\) these exhaust its roots and every one of them is simple — simplicity is a consequence of the count, not of the sign change. Figure 8 is this step.

🖼️ Figure 8

Step one of this appendix, for \(k=15\), an example where \(Q_k\) has two roots — with one root nothing would show that they are simple, which is half the statement. The smallest such \(k\) is \(12\), by Proposition 15; \(15\) is drawn because its two roots are further apart on the \(u\)-axis and the guides do not collide. Above, \(s_k\) on the interval, changing sign once between consecutive \(j\pi /k\); each change is a root, and they can be counted. Below, the invariant \(u(\theta )\) of (10), which climbs monotonically from \(0\) to \(\infty \), so each root above lands on a positive value of \(u\) and on a different one. The two halves of “real, positive and simple” are the two properties of this curve. The lower axis is logarithmic and clipped to the band where the roots fall; the curve leaves it at both ends, which is what “from \(0\) to \(\infty \)” means.

Step two: no fibre is cyclic, and not every fibre is reducible. Total reality then forces the discriminant \(-u^2(4u+27)\) to be a non-square in every real embedding, so no irreducible fibre has cyclic Galois group \(C_3\): every fibre is either reducible or has group \(S_3\). What remains is to exclude the case where every fibre is reducible. Writing \(Y\) for the root of the fibre cubic and eliminating \(u=Y^3/(1-Y)\), the roots of all fibres at once are the roots of

\[ P_k(Y)\; =\; (1-Y)^{d}\, Q_k\bigl(Y^3/(1-Y)\bigr)\; =\; \sum _{i=0}^{d}c_i\, Y^{3i}(1-Y)^{d-i}, \qquad Q_k=\sum _i c_iu^i, \]

a polynomial of degree \(3d\) and leading coefficient \(A=\mathrm{lc}(Q_k)\). Since \(\operatorname {disc}f_u{\lt}0\), each fibre has exactly one real root; moreover \(f_u(0)=-u{\lt}0\) and \(f_u(1)=1{\gt}0\), so that root lies in \((0,1)\). Hence \(P_k\) has exactly \(d\) real roots, all in \((0,1)\). If every fibre were reducible, those \(d\) real roots would form a rational factor of \(P_k\) — and this needs no irreducibility of \(Q_k\), which is Mirimanoff’s question and is not assumed anywhere here.

Lemma 21 the real roots form a factor
#
📕 p. 25📍 map❝ cite⚠ report

Suppose \(f_u\) is reducible over \({\mathbb {Q}}(u)\) for every root \(u\) of \(Q_k\), and let \(y(u)\in (0,1)\) be the real root of \(f_u\). Then the set \(\{ y(u):Q_k(u)=0\} \) is stable under \(\operatorname {Gal}(\overline{\mathbb {Q}}/{\mathbb {Q}})\), and the primitive integral multiple \(h\) of \(\prod _u(Y-y(u))\) lies in \({\mathbb {Z}}[Y]\), has degree \(d\), divides \(P_k\), and has leading coefficient \(B\mid A\).

Proof: in this note·Covers: not formalized·Cite: Lemma 21, p. 25, doi:10.5281/zenodo.22886543

↳ Used in: Proposition 13

Proof ▼

Every root of \(Q_k\) is real by step one, so every conjugate of \(u\) is real and \({\mathbb {Q}}(u)\) is totally real. A reducible cubic \(f_u\) has a root \(r\in {\mathbb {Q}}(u)\). For each embedding \(\sigma \) of \({\mathbb {Q}}(u)\), \(\sigma (r)\) is a real root of \(f_{\sigma (u)}\), whose discriminant is negative, so it is the only one: \(\sigma (r)=y(\sigma (u))\). Hence \(r=y(u)\), and the conjugates of \(y(u)\) are the values of \(y\) at the conjugates of \(u\). The \(y(u)\) are distinct, since \(u=y^3/(1-y)\) recovers \(u\), so the product has degree \(d\) and divides \(P_k\) in \({\mathbb {Q}}[Y]\); by Gauss’s lemma its primitive integral multiple divides \(P_k\) in \({\mathbb {Z}}[Y]\), whence \(B\mid A\).

Then \(h(0)\) and \(h(1)\) are nonzero integers, and \(1\le |h(0)h(1)|=B^2\prod y_i(1-y_i)\le A^2/4^{d}\), absurd once \(A{\lt}2^{d}\).

Conversely \(P_k\) irreducible forces every fibre to be \(S_3\), and the degrees close it in two lines. If \(y\) is a root of \(P_k\) then \(u=y^{3}/(1-y)\), so

\[ [{\mathbb {Q}}(y):{\mathbb {Q}}(u)]\le 3,\qquad [{\mathbb {Q}}(u):{\mathbb {Q}}]\le d . \]

Irreducibility gives \([{\mathbb {Q}}(y):{\mathbb {Q}}]=3d\), so both inequalities are equalities: \(Q_k\) is the minimal polynomial of \(u\), and \(f_u\) is irreducible over \({\mathbb {Q}}(u)\). Its discriminant is not a square there, by the opening of Step two, so its group is \(S_3\) and not \(C_3\).

Step three: \(A\le k\). What is left is to bound \(A\), and Waring’s formula does it at a single monomial — equivalently, one reads the extreme term of the classical expansion of \(x^k+y^k+z^k\) for \(x+y+z=0\) recalled in Section 6. Write \(s_k=\sum _{2a+3b=k}\gamma _{a,b}\, e_2^{\, a}e_3^{\, b}\) with \(e_1=0\), so that \(|\gamma _{a,b}|=k\, (a+b-1)!/(a!\, b!)\), and let \(\widetilde Q_k\) be that polynomial read in \(u=e_2^3/e_3^2\), of which \(Q_k\) is the primitive part. The top coefficient of \(\widetilde Q_k\) is the \(\gamma _{a,b}\) with \(b\) minimal, and \(3b=k-2a\) forces \(b\equiv k\pmod2\); there the factorials cancel outright,

\[ \begin{aligned} k\ \text{even}& :\quad b=0,\ \ a=\tfrac k2, & \qquad |\gamma _{a,b}|& =\frac{k\, (\tfrac k2-1)!}{(\tfrac k2)!\; 0!}=2;\\[3pt] k\ \text{odd}& :\quad b=1,\ \ a=\tfrac {k-3}2, & \qquad |\gamma _{a,b}|& =\frac{k\, (\tfrac {k-3}2)!}{(\tfrac {k-3}2)!\; 1!}=k. \end{aligned} \]

Passing to the primitive part divides every coefficient by one and the same content and leaves the degree alone, so \(A\) divides that number: \(A\mid 2\) for \(k\) even and \(A\mid k\) for \(k\) odd. Either way \(A\mid k\), and in particular \(A\le k\).

The inequality \(A{\lt}2^{d}\) therefore holds whenever \(k{\lt}2^{d}\), and that is arithmetic. Write \(k=6q+r\) with \(0\le r\le 5\), so that \(d=q-[r=1]\). For \(r\ne 1\) it is enough that \(6q+5{\lt}2^{q}\), which holds at \(q=6\) and is stable under \(q\mapsto q+1\); for \(r=1\) it is enough that \(6q+1{\lt}2^{q-1}\), which holds at \(q=7\) and is stable likewise. So \(k{\lt}2^{d}\) for every \(k\ge 38\), and among the \(k\le 37\) with \(d{\gt}0\) the bound \(k{\lt}2^{d}\) fails at twenty-nine; only at those can \(A{\lt}2^{d}\) fail.

Step four: the remaining \(k\), by certificate. Those twenty-nine are settled, together with every other \(k\) in the same range, by exact certificates rather than left as a finite computation not carried out: \(P_k\) is irreducible over \({\mathbb {Q}}\) for all \(6\le k\le 46\) with \(d{\gt}0\), forty cases, each certified by a prime modulo which \(P_k\) is still irreducible. The certificates are printed in Table 3, because a certificate one has to take on trust is not a certificate. Proposition 13 is therefore unconditional for every \(k\), with no measured input anywhere in the chain.

Measured: For every \(6\le k\le 46\) with \(\deg Q_k{\gt}0\): the \(d\) roots of \(Q_k\) real, positive and simple by Sturm sequences; \(Q_k(0)\ne 0\); \(P_k\) of degree \(3d\) with exactly \(d\) real roots, all in \((0,1)\); and \(P_k\) irreducible over \({\mathbb {Q}}\), with the witness prime printed for each. The seven exceptions to \(A{\lt}2^{d}\) at the measured value of \(A\) are \(k=6,9,10,15,21,33,35\), of which \(k=6,10\) are equality cases. The proof above uses only \(A\le k\), which is weaker: it leaves twenty-nine exceptions rather than seven, and those are checked to be the values \(k\le 37\) with \(d{\gt}0\) and \(k\ge 2^{d}\), all inside the certified range. The two lists, the raw leading coefficient \(2\) or \(k\), and the divisibility \(A\mid k\) are each verified by a separate route for \(3\le k\le 400\). See gates/P3d_s3_certificados.py and gates/P3d_lc_Qk.py.

B The four strands, told by their people

Figure 2 draws four lines of work that never meet until this note needs all four. Read by years it is a diagram; read by people it is better, and the pieces below say which section of the note each one hangs from. Nothing here is needed to follow the mathematics. Everything here has been checked against the source named with it, and four attractive stories about the same people were found to be legend or to rest on paraphrase and are excluded deliberately rather than dropped in silence.

B.1 The identity was found while refereeing (Section 6)

On Monday 16 September 1839 the Académie des sciences heard a commission report. Its heading names the commissioners and, in the French convention, which of them wrote it: “Commissaires, MM. Liouville, Cauchy rapporteur.” The subject was Lamé’s memoir proving Fermat’s Last Theorem for the exponent seven, and the report approves it — “les savants apprendront avec plaisir qu’il est parvenu effectivement au but qu’il s’était proposé d’atteindre”.

The interesting part is what the two referees did next. Rather than stop at a verdict they asked whether the lemma Lamé had used might be a special case of something more general; they found that it was; and they judged the answer worth a detour in their own report — “un théorème d’analyse qui nous semble assez curieux pour mériter d’être indiqué dans ce rapport”  [ 13 ] . The theorem is the factorisation \((x+y)^n-x^n-y^n=n\, xy(x+y)(x^2+xy+y^2)^{b}E_n(x,y)\), with \(b\in \{ 0,1,2\} \) as in Section 6, and \(E_n\) is the family whose \(S_3\) quotient Section 6 evaluates. An object produced as a by-product of auditing somebody else’s proof has outlived the proof it was auditing: Lamé’s exponent seven was superseded within a year, and \(E_n\)’s irreducibility is open in 2026.

The two men return eight years later on the other side of the same subject. In March 1847 Lamé announced a general proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem by factoring into linear factors over the cyclotomic integers; the announcement did not survive the session, and both his and the competing programme foundered on the arithmetic of those integers. Lamé wrote to Dirichlet in June of that year — “Les sages avis de Liouville m’ont désillusionné; j’ai rougi de ma folle équipée”  [ 8 ] .

B.2 Mirimanoff conjectured twice, in two subjects (Section 8)

Dmitry Mirimanoff conjectured in 1903 that \(E_n\) is irreducible over \({\mathbb {Q}}\) for \(n\) prime  [ 32 ] . That is still open, and Section 8 records why it is a question about exactly the polynomials our Theorem 12 evaluates. The same Mirimanoff, in Geneva in 1917, wrote the paper that introduced the cumulative hierarchy and the distinction between well-founded and ill-founded sets — the idea that became the axiom of foundation. Two conjectures in two subjects, one of which is now a standard axiom and the other of which is still open after a hundred and twenty years.

B.3 Mann proved his first theorem with no academic position (Section 2)

The criterion of Section 2 rests on Mann’s theorem  [ 24 ] on relations between roots of unity, which he published in 1965. It is not the work he is remembered for. Mann emigrated from Vienna in 1938; in New York he earned his living for several years primarily by tutoring; and in 1941, with no academic post, he proved the Schnirelmann–Landau conjecture on the density of sums of sets of integers, a problem on which Landau, Khinchin, Besicovitch, Schur and Brauer had obtained partial results over the preceding decade. His interest in it had been aroused by Brauer’s lectures at New York University — that is, by one of the people who had nearly solved it. The American Mathematical Society gave him the Cole Prize in 1946. He is also, separately, the Mann of the Mann–Whitney test.

B.4 Higman posed the PORC question from outside the war (Section 6)

Graham Higman’s 1960 paper  [ 10 ] asks whether the number of groups of order \(p^n\) is polynomial on residue classes in \(p\) — the PORC conjecture, proved for \(n\le 7\) and open for \(n\ge 8\), and the question Section 6 answers in the negative for our counts. His mathematical career had been interrupted: he registered as a conscientious objector and served the war in the Meteorological Office, in Northern Ireland and Gibraltar. He returned to become Waynflete Professor at Oxford from 1960 to 1984, supervised more than fifty doctoral students, and founded the Journal of Algebra.

B.5 The Hungarian strand, and a prize shaped like the Fano plane (Remark 10)

Vandermonde sets were introduced by András Gács and Zsuzsa Weiner in 2003, in a paper about arcs; Sziklai and Takáts classified the super-Vandermonde ones in 2008  [ 45 ] , and their Theorem 1.12 is what Remark 10 recovers by a different route. All of them belong to the finite-geometry school built at Eötvös Loránd University in Budapest. Gács died in 2009, at forty; his family endowed a prize for young mathematics teachers in his name, whose trophy is a model of the Fano plane.

B.6 The Conway of Conway–Jones (Section 2)

The sharpening of Mann’s theorem from five terms on, which we quote but do not need, is Conway–Jones  [ 23 ] . It is the John Horton Conway — the paper is item 115 of his own bibliography — and the co-author is not an anonymous initial either: A. J. Jones is Antonia Jane Jones (1943–2010), who took a Cambridge doctorate on sums of roots of unity, the subject of the paper, and who signs it from Royal Holloway College while Conway signs from D. P. M. M. S. The two standard records of her thesis disagree, and we report the disagreement rather than choose: the Mathematics Genealogy Project gives Sums of roots of unity and Diophantine approximation, 1969, supervised by Harold Davenport and J. W. S. Cassels, and Wikipedia gives Sums of roots of unity and cyclic overlattices, 1968. We could not find the thesis itself, and the paper does not cite it.

The paper is worth reading to the end for a reason that has nothing to do with our use of it. Having built the machinery for vanishing sums of roots of unity, the last page spends it on a piece of elementary geometry: a triangle all of whose edges are rational and all of whose angles are rational multiples of \(\pi \) must be equilateral. The proof is three lines, and its engine is the step that \((k,n)=1\Rightarrow k\equiv \pm 1\pmod n\) forces \(n\in \{ 1,2,3,4,6\} \) — bookkeeping over small cyclotomic degrees, of the same flavour as the criterion of Section 2. Jones later left number theory altogether and became Professor of Evolutionary and Neural Computing at Cardiff, with sixteen doctoral students to her name.

B.7 The gap in our list is where \(\Delta \) lives (Corollary 17)

Corollary 17 says that \(C_k(3,p)\) is elementary exactly when \(\dim M_{2k}(\mathrm{SL}_2({\mathbb {Z}}))=1\), and the four weights are \(6,8,10,14\), with forms \(E_6\), \(E_8\), \(E_{10}\), \(E_{14}\). The list is easier to remember by what is missing from it: weight \(12\). And the reason weight \(12\) is missing is a single function.

The dimension of \(M_w\) grows by one every twelve, and the first place it reaches two is \(w=12\), because that is where the first cusp form appears:

\[ \Delta (q)=q\prod _{n\ge 1}(1-q^{n})^{24}=\sum _{n\ge 1}\tau (n)q^{n} . \]

So \(\dim M_{12}=2\) and our \(k=6\) is not elementary — it is the first \(k\) where the count needs a cubic. Weight \(14\) then returns to dimension one, and the reason is exact rather than approximate: every cusp form of weight \(w\) is \(\Delta \) times a form of weight \(w-12\), that is \(S_w=\Delta \, M_{w-12}\), and \(M_2=0\), so \(S_{14}=0\). There is no room for a cusp form in weight \(14\) because there is nothing in weight \(2\) to multiply \(\Delta \) by. That is the whole reason \(k=7\) joins \(3,4,5\). The exceptional residue class \(k\equiv 1\pmod6\) of Proposition 15, which looks like an arithmetic accident when one only counts solutions of \(2a+3b=k\), is that same lag seen from the other side.

Ramanujan wrote the coefficients \(\tau (n)\) down in 1916 and conjectured, on the evidence of a table, that they are multiplicative and satisfy \(|\tau (p)|\le 2p^{11/2}\)  [ 29 ] . Mordell proved the multiplicativity the following year  [ 30 ] . The bound waited until Deligne derived it in 1974 from the Weil conjectures  [ 31 ] — which is the same Weil-weight formalism that Section 3 uses to decide our length-four strata, at weight eleven instead of weight one: each two-dimensional weight-one pair contributes at most \(2\sqrt p\), so for a genus-\(g\) curve the whole trace is bounded by \(2g\sqrt p\), and the two-dimensional representation attached to \(\Delta \) is bounded by \(2p^{11/2}\).

B.8 Twelve edges, and then years with nothing to show (Section 7)

The story Section 7 points at is worth telling with its dates, because it is the same shape as this note at a much larger scale. Kontsevich conjectured in 1997 that the number of points of a graph hypersurface over \({\mathbb {F}}_q\) is a (quasi-)polynomial in \(q\). Stembridge then verified it by computer  [ 46 ] , for every graph with at most twelve edges; that is the whole of what was reachable, and it all agreed. In 2003 Belkale and Brosnan  [ 1 ] proved the conjecture false, and false in the strongest available sense: for large graphs the counting functions are of general type.

The part that is easy to miss is what happened next, which is nothing. Their method builds graphs with very large numbers of edges, so for years after the conjecture was known to be false, no explicit counterexample was known; the first ones came later, from two independent constructions, and those of  [ 3 ] are graphs of \(\phi ^4\) theory whose counting functions carry a modular form of a singular K3 surface. A statement can be refuted long before anything can be shown.

That gap is the reason this note is built the way it is. Appendix A could have said that \(P_k\) is irreducible for every \(k\) it was able to test; instead it proves \(A{\lt}2^{d}\) for all \(k\ge 38\) and prints forty certificates for the rest, each one a prime a reader can check without believing anything of ours. And Section B.10 is the same lesson in miniature, on our own data: four values of \(k\) in a row with \(Q_k\) monic, and the fifth is not. There the counterexample was the very next case. Kontsevich’s was out of reach for years.

Measured: The two dates and the twelve edges against the abstract of  [ 3 ] , which states them, and the absence of an explicit counterexample against its introduction, which says so in those words. Nothing here rests on a secondary account.

B.9 Four integers for every extension at once (Section 8)

Absolute simplicity is a question about infinitely many fields at once. An abelian surface that is simple over \({\mathbb {F}}_p\) may split over \({\mathbb {F}}_{p^m}\), and no search over \(m\), however long, can show that it never does. Section 8 settles it for \(J(D)\) with four comparisons of integers at each of two primes, and the theorem that makes that possible was not written for anything like our question.

Howe and Zhu  [ 9 ] set out to prove that over every field, and in every dimension, there is an abelian variety that stays simple over the algebraic closure. An absolutely simple variety stays simple over every extension field, so it is enough to treat the prime fields; over \({\mathbb {Q}}\), as they note, examples in every dimension were already known from Mori and Zarhin, so what was left was \({\mathbb {F}}_p\). Their Theorem 6 is the tool for dimension two: it reads the answer off the characteristic polynomial of Frobenius of a simple ordinary surface, and it gives, in their words, “a very short proof” of that case.

The list of four conditions is short, and part of the reason is one already met at the end of  [ 23 ] . Their proof takes the least \(d\) for which \({\mathbb {Q}}(\alpha ^{d})\) is a proper subfield of the quartic CM field \({\mathbb {Q}}(\alpha )\), \(\alpha \) a root of the Weil polynomial, and shows that either the Weil polynomial is a polynomial in \(T^2\) or \(T^4\), or \({\mathbb {Q}}(\alpha )\) is obtained from an imaginary quadratic field by adjoining a primitive \(d\)-th root of unity. If that root of unity generated a field of degree larger than two it would have to generate all of \({\mathbb {Q}}(\alpha )\), which the proof rules out; so it lies in a quadratic field, and a root of unity in a quadratic field has order \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), \(4\) or \(6\). The splitting degrees \(2\) and \(4\) can come from the first alternative, the Weil polynomial being a polynomial in \(T^2\) or \(T^4\); the degrees \(3\) and \(6\) can only come from the second, as orders of roots of unity in an imaginary quadratic field. That short list is the same phenomenon, \(\varphi (d)\le 2\), as the \(n\in \{ 1,2,3,4,6\} \) that gives Conway and Jones their equilateral triangle.

Measured: The aim of  [ 9 ] , the reduction to prime fields, the attribution to Mori and Zarhin, the phrase “a very short proof” and the structure of the proof of Theorem 6 read off the arXiv version of the paper, math/0002205, its introduction and Section 4; the four conditions and the splitting degrees against the statement of Theorem 6 there.

B.10 A pattern that is not one (Section 6)

The values \(k=11,17,23,29\) give \(Q_{11}=u-1\), \(Q_{17}=u^2-5u+1\), \(Q_{23}=u^3-12u^2+14u-1\) and \(Q_{29}=u^4-22u^3+66u^2-30u+1\): monic, with constant term \(\pm 1\). It is tempting to read that as a property of the class \(k\equiv 5\pmod6\). It is not: the next member is

\[ Q_{35}(u)=35u^5-1225u^4+7007u^3-8580u^2+1925u-35, \]

primitive but not monic. Helou  [ 16 , p. 53 ] explains why \(k\) prime gives a monic \(Q_k\): \(T_k\) is monic over \({\mathbb {Q}}\) always, and lies in \({\mathbb {Z}}[X]\) when \(k\) is prime. \(T_k\) is defined for odd \(k\), and for odd \(k\) our \(Q_k\) is its primitive integral form, so \(Q_k\) is monic exactly when \(T_k\) is already integral, and in particular whenever \(k\) is prime. That \(35\) breaks the pattern is measured, not explained. The converse is not a theorem we have. For odd \(k\le 400\) the monic \(Q_k\) are exactly those of prime \(k\) — for odd \(k\le 40\), \(11,13,17,19,23,29,31,37\) and not \(35\) — but that is a measurement; and for even \(k\) it is false, since \(Q_8\), \(Q_{16}\), \(Q_{32}\), … are monic too. See gates/P3d_lc_Qk.py. Searching the leading and constant coefficients turns up no usable OEIS entry, and the variable content makes such searches fragile in any case.

Measured: Every quotation above checked against its source: the two French passages of Section B.1 and the approval of Lamé’s memoir character by character against the Comptes rendus themselves; Lamé’s letter against  [ 8 ] ; the statements about Mann against the Ohio State University departmental memorial and those about Higman against his obituary and the Royal Society biographical memoir. The affiliations, submission dates and reference list of  [ 23 ] , and its closing theorem on rational triangles, read off the published pages; the two conflicting records of Jones’s thesis are reported as conflicting because we could not settle them. In Section B.7 the mathematics — \(\dim M_{12}=2\), \(\dim M_{14}=1\), and the product expansion of \(\Delta \) — is checked in gates/P3d_familia_Qk.py and follows from  [ 28 ] , which we have read; the three historical attributions to Ramanujan, Mordell and Deligne are cited for priority only, carry nothing the argument uses, and are not claimed as read. Four further stories about the same people are excluded as legend or as resting on paraphrase, deliberately rather than in silence.

Table 3. The forty certificates behind Proposition 13. For each $k$ with $\deg Q_k>0$ in the range, $d=\deg Q_k$, $A=\mathrm{lc}(Q_k)$, and $p$ is a prime modulo which $P_k$ — of degree $3d$ — remains irreducible, which proves it irreducible over ${\mathbb{Q}}$. Each row is checkable in one line of any computer algebra system and requires nothing of ours to be believed. Shade of $A$ is the margin $2^{d}/A$ by which the inequality holds — dark where it barely does, pale where it holds by orders of magnitude — and the tinted rows are the seven where it does not hold at all. The two codes together are the shape of the argument: the margin grows exponentially in $k$ while $A\le k$ grows at most linearly, so the tinted rows can only occur early, and they do. The table is generated by gates/P3d_s3_certificados.py, not typed.
